# Timeline, station and map sources

Research register assembled **23 September 2026** for the eight systems then in the repository; the Chengdu, Beijing, Nanjing and Chongqing sections were added on **24 September 2026** from new research, the Seoul section on **25 September 2026**, and the Xi'an section on **27 September 2026**. Later corrections are dated where they are described.

This file preserves references recovered from earlier research and adds newly located corroboration. For the first twelve systems and Xi'an it indexes **every current event entry and every legend line**, including historical predecessors, trams, light rail and gondolas; the Seoul section summarises its sources by topic instead. It also records sources for station/transfer identities, kilometres, drawn geography and logos.

The Tokyo, Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Guangzhou line-history references were largely recovered from earlier map-building research. Most Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei, Singapore and Foshan line-history links were located again for this register; they should not be represented as a recovered original bibliography. The existing spec also preserved several original Hong Kong and geographic references.

**Coverage is not the same as verification.** Some entries still have only a secondary chronology, some exact days are placeholders, and some historical distances/coordinates are estimates. Those limitations are recorded below; this is not a claim that every existing value has a reliable primary citation. No timeline data or geometry was changed while assembling this register.

## How to read and maintain this file

- **Recovered** means the reference was found in the existing spec, earlier research files or their bibliographies. It does not mean the original author of every asset can be proven to have used it.
- **New** means a reference located for this register; it corroborates existing data rather than proving its original provenance.
- **Recovered citation** links preserve useful original notices and contemporary reports cited by the earlier research. They have not all been independently reopened; a link is not a claim of successful retrieval. Archives and WeChat in particular may block automated access.
- **Secondary chronology** means a line/station history, usually Wikipedia. It is useful for locating dated primary evidence, but must not settle a disputed day merely because the repo agrees with it.
- **Unresolved / unverified day** identifies a specific claim that still needs evidence. A source for a line opening does not automatically substantiate a rename, delayed station or paid-area change listed in the same event.
- Event-table descriptions below are an inventory copied from the repository, **not quotations from the linked sources**. Sources apply only to their stated subject. The table deliberately preserves questionable entries so they can be corrected in the data after verification.
- Prefer operator notices and dated maps; then government records, contemporary reporting and scholarly histories; then secondary timelines and their footnotes. A planned opening, trial without public passengers, construction completion or ceremony is not necessarily first passenger service.

### What needs a source

| Stored fact                                                       | Evidence to use                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `events.json`: each date and each description                     | Event index below; resolve each independent claim, not just the first description on the date.                                              |
| `lines.json`: historical names and start/end dates                | Line histories and dated naming notices; corporate establishment, service takeover and public renaming can occur on different days.         |
| SVG track labels: opening, removal, reassignment                  | Opening/withdrawal notices and historical route diagrams; end dates are exclusive, so first absent day may be the day after last operation. |
| SVG station labels: name, opening, relocation, marker replacement | Line station tables plus station-specific histories and operator plans; a marker upgrade is not a newly opened physical station.            |
| SVG `data-lines`, connectors and station identity                 | Dated interchange diagrams and fare-area notices. Walking connection, continuous fare and shared paid area are different facts.             |
| SVG `data-km`                                                     | Published operating section length, with rounding/allocation documented; not the length of the Bézier path.                                 |
| SVG route/station/water coordinates                               | Original map provenance, engineering alignment and mapped geographic features; modern geometry does not establish historical geometry.      |
| Colours, logos and compact interchange shapes                     | Operator wayfinding/map and original artwork. These are presentation choices, not extra historical events.                                  |

The date boundaries in the indexed `map.svg` files (station/track labels and `data-lines`) and their `lines.json` legends were compared with their `events.json`: **none fall on a date absent from the event index**. This checks coverage of dates, not correctness or completeness of every description. Source links for the line station tables also cover intermediate stations omitted from event prose.

Use [the map data spec](map-data-spec.md#11-sources-and-verification) for scope and parsing. This is a build history: maintenance, accidents and temporary operating suspensions normally do not erase built track. Lines are drawn exactly when the public could ride them, including public previews, free trial rides, experience weeks, voucher rides, sightseeing, trial and restricted-access service (spec §7). When a preview came before the opening, both are events: the preview names its kind of service, the line is drawn from its first public rides onward with no gap and no "rides end" event, and the opening is recorded as its own event even when it changes nothing on the map. A preview followed by more than a year without service is left off the map; the line then appears at its regular opening. Test runs without passengers, ceremonies and VIP rides, and open days without rides are noted but not drawn.

## Accuracy gaps to keep visible

1. **Hong Kong:** 1913 Sheung Shui halt and other early KCR/Sha Tau Kok halts are not fully inventoried; Hung Hom 1921 closure, Kowloon Tong 1982 opening and 1996 names need exact-day evidence. Several 1960s rename dates encode only a known year. Historical KCR geometry and Light Rail stage lengths are estimates. Under the spec §7 rule the MTR's 1979-09-30 open day, Light Rail's free rides (1988-09-14–16), West Rail's charity trial days (2003-12-16–18), the East Tsim Sha Tsui extension's one-day trial (2004-10-17, zh-wiki only) and Ma On Shan Rail's charity ride day (2004-12-19) are drawn from their first public day and stay on the map; each opening (1979-10-01, 1988-09-18, 2003-12-20, 2004-10-24, 2004-12-21) is its own event. The Airport Railway's 1998-06-12 public open day is not drawn because it is not known whether trains were ridden.
2. **Shanghai:** early surface-alignment replacements, paid-area passage dates and exact English naming rollouts need stronger primary evidence. The English timeline and other histories disagree on the first Line 3 day. Under the spec §7 rule Line 2 appears on 1999-09-20 (organised visits, then sightseeing; regular service 2000-06-11), the Expo Line on 2010-04-20 (invited-visitor trial days; all Expo visitors from 2010-05-01) and Songjiang Tram 2 on 2018-12-20 (free trial rides, continuing into its 2018-12-26 opening), each later step with its own event; the October 1999 start of public Line 2 sightseeing has no exact day. Two openings may be earlier than recorded but keep their dates because the first public day is not established: Line 1's southern section (1993-05-28) had one-train sightseeing from 28 January or 9 April 1993 (sources disagree, continuity unknown); its Xujiahui – Shanghai Railway Station section (1995-04-10) reportedly had sightseeing from 28 December 1994 (secondary sources only); the Maglev's 2003 sightseeing pause (2003-03-10 – 09-19, from its published timetable and the 2004 yearbook) is not drawn. Line 8's 16 September 2007 non-stop ride for 260 invited residents at a Transport Week ceremony is not counted.
3. **Taipei:** extension dates do not by themselves prove when modern combined line names became official. Some stored section kilometres differ from operator historical tables. Muzha (1996-02-27), the Tucheng extension (2006-05-27, Banqiao–Tucheng, one day), the Neihu section (2009-06-29 – 07-01), the Airport MRT (2017-02-16) and the Circular Line (2020-01-19) appear with their free public trial rides, and their openings (1996-03-28, 2006-05-31, 2009-07-04, 2017-03-02, 2020-01-31) are separate events (spec §7). The Xiaobitan branch's 24 September 2004 free trial ride is uncited and not used. The Xinyi Line eastern extension (Xiangshan – Guangci/Fengtian Temple) opened on 2026-08-30 without a public preview; the new station's position is projected from OpenStreetMap through the existing fit, and the Tamsui–Xinyi Line's 31.1 km adds the published 1.4 km to the stored 29.7 km rather than a published line total.
4. **Singapore:** since 2009 most new stages had a one-day open house or public preview with free rides a few days to three weeks before regular service; each is drawn from that day onwards, with no gap before regular service, and followed by an opening event (spec §7). The 2009 Circle Line open house (23 May, Bartley–Marymount) and the 13 January 2012 Circle Line extension open house are attested as having free rides only by a blog and keep their regular dates; the NEL 2003 preview lead and pre-2009 open days are unconfirmed (the 1987–1990 open days were station viewings without trains). Early East–West naming and exact section kilometres need checking beyond a current network map.
5. **Shenzhen:** January 2025 SIAT/SUAT rename day and December 2025 Grand Theater passage day are not established. Simplified tram/Skyshuttle interchange markers deliberately compress real walking distances.
6. **Hangzhou:** October 2019 English Yuhang rename is month-only. Airport/railway-station continuous fares must not be mistaken for physically joined paid areas. Lines 1 and 2 appear with their free trial rides (2012-11-18 – 21 and 2014-11-18 – 22), stay on the map through regular service on 24 November, and that opening is its own event; which Line 1 stations the 2012 rides served is inferred from the opening arrangement.
7. **Guangzhou/Foshan:** May/November 2006 and September 2021 naming rollouts lack exact days. Under the spec §7 rule Line 1 appears with its paid sightseeing services (Xilang–Huangsha 1997-06-28, Huangsha–Guangzhou East 1999-02-16); the line then closed for final testing from 1999-03-03 until regular service on 1999-06-28, a pause the map does not draw (spec §7), so Line 1 stays on the map from 1997. When the 1997 sightseeing on Xilang–Huangsha ended (possibly by January 1999) is not established. The Guangfo Line appears with its trial rides (2010-10-28 – 29) and stays through its 2010-11-03 opening. Huangpu Tram 2's preview (2020-12-29 – 2021-01-03) was followed by over four years without service, so it is left off and the section appears at its 2025-06-20 opening. Line 12 length definitions differ between sources.
8. **Chengdu:** the July 2023 English renaming batch, the Jincheng Plaza English forms and the 2020 Chengdu Academy of Governance rename lack exact days (latest attested days are used). Line 2's east section was cut back from 2025-12-20 and returned on 2026-09-28 on its rebuilt alignment ([川观新闻](https://cbgc.scol.com.cn/news/7991007)). The new Longquanyi Railway Station between Chengdu Academy of Governance and Damianpu was not part of the reopening; add it when it opens. Line 8 phase 2, Line 10 phase 3 and several phase lengths are allocated from published totals. Lines 1 and 2 appear with their free trial rides (2010-09-10 – 12, 2012-09-01 – 03), stay on the map through their openings (2010-09-27, 2012-09-16), which are separate events; Line 1's trial dates rest on the zh-wiki chronology.
9. **Beijing:** Line 1 appears on 1971-01-15 and the Olympic branch on 2008-07-19 with restricted-access service (spec §7); their openings to all passengers (1972-12-27, 2008-10-09) and Line 1's formal opening (1981-09-15) are separate events. Exact days for Lixin/Gongzhufen, Bajiaocun/Bajiao Amusement Park, Xinhua Jie/Heping Men and Gucheng Lu/Gucheng renames remain unresolved. Those markers use current names; the map does not claim a complete day-resolved rename history. Historical Xi’erqi placement and section kilometres remain approximate. See the Beijing section for decisions and scope.
10. **Nanjing, Chongqing and Seoul:** their remaining evidence gaps are listed in their own sections (Nanjing's 2005 sightseeing extensions and subtitle renames; Chongqing's Xiejiawan (2005, display bound) and Zengjiayan (2005-06-15, zh-wiki only) opening days and rename rollouts; Seoul's undated romanization and subtitle changes). Seoul's GTX-A citizen inspection rides (March 2024, days unknown) and reported Shinbundang free rides (October 2011, fan wiki only) are not drawn.
11. **Xi'an:** the 2025 rename day (2025-12-22, first reported signage; zh.wikipedia says 2025-12-29), the paid-area status of 双寨's Line 3/14 transfer, the English names used on the Airport Intercity in 2019–21 and the undated numbered-road spelling change (`5-LU` → `5 LU`) remain open; see [its section](#xian). Line 1's 2013 trial-ride ticket distribution is inferred from its scale.
12. **Across systems:** a published present-day total does not prove each historical `data-km` allocation, and a geographic SVG is not a survey. Original artwork provenance remains incompletely recovered for several older systems.

## Hong Kong — MTR / KCR (`hongkong`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/hongkong/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/hongkong/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/hongkong/map.svg).

Scope follows the MTR network map, which includes the High Speed Rail's Hong Kong section and Light Rail (drawn as tracks only), plus the operator's own Ngong Ping 360 (spec §8). KCR lines are the predecessors of today's East Rail, Tuen Ma and Light Rail. Station tooltips show `kcr` until the 2007-12-02 merger and `mtr` from then on (spec §5); the merger's event is that day's renames.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [KCRC: history][p-mtr-kcrc] — **New**. Operator chronology, KCR opening, 1913 Sheung Shui halt, electrification, Light Rail and later projects; distinguish ceremonies from first passenger operation.
- [KCR annual report 1921, paragraph 19][p-mtr-1921] — **Recovered**. Original government report, hosted by Histsyn; Hung Hom / Ho Man Tin halt evidence. Does not settle the repo's exact Hung Hom closure day.
- [KCR annual report 1935, paragraphs 59 and 102][p-mtr-1935] — **Recovered**. Che Kung Miu experimental halt, 16 November 1935; location at Bridge 12.
- [KCR annual report 1936, paragraph 41][p-mtr-1936] — **Recovered**. Che Kung Miu withdrawal, 1 October 1936.
- [KCR annual report 1976][p-mtr-1976] — **Recovered**. 1975 Kowloon terminal relocation and historical route context.
- [Hong Kong Railway Museum: Fanling–Sha Tau Kok Branch][p-mtr-stk-museum] — **Recovered**. Museum account and historical alignment/station illustrations; stronger provenance than a modern inferred route.
- [R. J. Phillips: Sha Tau Kok Branch, a study 1911–1928][p-mtr-stk-study] — **New**. Historical study, not an operator notice; consult its primary citations for partial opening and closure dates.
- [Contemporary Light Rail opening notice (newspaper scan)][p-mtr-lr-preview] — **Recovered**. 14–16 September 1988 free public rides (drawn as a preview), no service on the 17th, fare-paying regular service from 18 September (the opening). Forum hosts the scan; the source is the newspaper notice.
- [Government daily information bulletin, 6 November 1991][p-mtr-lr-1991] — **Recovered**. Reports the extension opening on the preceding Sunday, 3 November; not 17 November.
- [LegCo: commissioning new railways, December 2003][p-mtr-lr-2003] — **Recovered**. Light Rail extensions opened 7 December; West Rail commissioning context.
- [MTR annual report 2018, Hong Kong transport operations][p-mtr-xrl-2018] — **Recovered**. Hong Kong high-speed rail opening, 23 September 2018.
- [MTR business overview][p-mtr-km] — **Recovered**. Published route lengths; Hong Kong XRL 25.7 km versus rounded 26 km project descriptions. Current totals do not certify every historical section allocation.
- [LegCo: XRL project report and alignment, December 2016][p-mtr-xrl-plan] — **Recovered**. Engineering alignment; Hong Kong section extent. The drawn continuation into Shenzhen is context, not additional Hong Kong kilometres.
- [MTR corporate profile][p-mtr-merger] — **New**. Rail merger on 2 December 2007; operator identity context for KCR/MTR labels.
- [MTR annual reports and results archive][p-mtr-reports] — **New**. Primary archive for modern openings, names and mileage. An archive index is a research route, not proof of an individual date.
- [MTR investor presentation, January 2018][p-mtr-island-west] — **New**. Slide 35: West Island Line 28 December 2014, Sai Ying Pun 29 March 2015, Kwun Tong extension 23 October 2016 and South Island Line 28 December 2016.
- [MTR PR030/22: East Rail cross-harbour opening][p-mtr-erl-2022] — **New**. Passenger service from 15 May 2022, Hung Hom–Admiralty and Exhibition Centre station.
- [EMSD: Tuen Ma Line Phase 1 opening][p-mtr-tml-2020] — **New**. 14 February 2020 and the distinction between Phase 1 and the later full line.

### Historical coverage and outstanding evidence

- Sha Tau Kok is split at its public openings: Fanling–Shek Chung Au on 1911-12-21,
  then Sha Tau Kok on 1912-04-01; both close on 1928-04-01. The opening notices are
  transcribed in the [branch history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sha_Tau_Kok_Branch).
  [KCRC](https://www.kcrc.com/en/about-kcrc/history.html) gives the full route as 11.6 km.
  The map includes Fanling, Hung Leng, Wo Hang, Shek Chung Au and Sha Tau Kok.
  Lung Yeuk Tau's location/closure and the five February 1916 halts (Kwan Tei, Ma Mei Ha,
  Loi Tung, Tai Long, San Tsuen) remain unresolved; do not invent exact days or positions.
- Che Kung Miu is a separate historical halt, not the present Che Kung Temple station.
  KCR's [1935 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/AR1935.html), paragraphs 59 and 102,
  records its opening on November 16 near Bridge 12; the
  [1936 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/AR1936.html), paragraph 41, records closure
  on October 1. Historical geometry follows the existing map's approximate scale.
- The original Kowloon terminus and Chatham Road approach are separate from East Tsim Sha Tsui's
  2004 tunnel. The [1975 replacement](https://www.histsyn.com/2023/01/kcr1976.html) and
  [1981 Beacon Hill Tunnel switchover](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Hill_Tunnel_(Hong_Kong)>)
  retain the modern track geometry. Short switchover gaps are collapsed under §7.
- High Speed Rail's Hong Kong section opens on 2018-09-23, per
  [MTR's 2018 report](https://www.mtr.com.hk/archive/corporate/en/investor/annual2018/E110.pdf).
  Its 25.7 km value uses [MTR's business overview](https://www.mtr.com.hk/archive/corporate/en/publications/images/business_overview_e.pdf)
  rather than the rounded 26 km project length. Its curve follows the
  [published alignment](https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr16-17/english/panels/tp/tp_rdp/papers/tp_rdp20161209cb4-243-9-e.pdf)
  through Shek Kong and Mai Po, continuing towards Futian and off the map's northern edge.
  The Shenzhen continuation supplies geographic context from the Hong Kong opening date;
  the kilometres and station count cover only the Hong Kong section. No boundary station is added.
- This is **not yet a complete historical inventory**. KCRC records a Sheung Shui halt in 1913;
  the map still starts at the dated 1930 station opening. KCR's
  [1921 report](https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/AR1921.html), paragraph 19, also records a
  Ho Mun Tin halt without an exact opening day. Both need dated timetables and location evidence.
  The old Hung Hom closure (June 13 versus September 15/16, 1921) and the precise 1996 renaming
  date remain disputed; the existing dates are retained, not newly certified.
- Light Rail tracks now distinguish the 1988-09-14–16 free-ride preview, the 1988-09-18 opening, 1988-09-24 northern/estate
  branches, 1991-11-03 southern extension, 1992-02-02 eastern/Sam Shing extensions,
  1993-01-10 Tin Shui branch, 1995-03-26 Tin Shui Wai Terminus extension, and 2003-12-07
  northern/eastern Tin Shui Wai extensions. Existing modern curves and stroke widths are retained.
  The [contemporary opening notice](https://att.hkitalk.net/HKiTalk2/data/attachment/forum/202303/04/105705khyhdansbyz8h0gs.jpeg)
  lists free public rides on routes 610/611/612 on September 14–16, no service on the 17th, and
  fare-paying service from September 18. Under §7 the line is drawn from September 14 and stays through the
  September 18 opening (the no-service day is not drawn as a closure); both dates have events. Routes 505/506 and the
  "whole network except 507 and 512" date of September 25 in the same notice are not yet
  reconciled with the 1988-09-24 branch date. Route 506's September 23 introduction uses
  existing track; its individual stops are outside this map's Light Rail scope.
  The [government's November 6, 1991 bulletin](https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/daily-information-bulletin-1990s-1991_13.html)
  says the southern extension opened the previous Sunday (November 3), consistent with the
  November 4 newspaper cited by [Goodview Garden's history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/豐景園站).
  This takes precedence over the November 17 date in several English station articles.
  The [stop chronology](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_Rail_(MTR)#Stops>) identifies the 1992,
  1993 and 1995 stages; [LegCo's commissioning report](https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr03-04/english/panels/tp/tp_rdp/papers/tp_rdp1219cb1-613-1e.pdf)
  confirms December 7, 2003. Tin Shui's former terminus position is interpolated on the existing
  curve; stop-scale turning loops and the 2002–03 grade-separation realignments remain simplified.
  Stage kilometres are the estimates described under the SVG notes below.
- Existing route kilometres are estimates: distinguish route length, construction length
  and the operator's exclusion of duplicated sections before recalibrating individual paths.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

The original SVG carried the title “MTR system map in English released to the public domain” (removed in the September 2026 normalisation, since spec §3 bans `<title>`); its exact upstream Commons revision has not been recovered. Do not treat that embedded statement as full provenance for later additions. The background geography was replaced on 23 September 2026 using the sources below; the KCR/Sha Tau Kok reconstructions still require historical maps rather than modern track data.

- Coastlines and islands: © [OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), data under [ODbL 1.0](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/), from [Geofabrik's Guangdong extract, including Hong Kong and Macau](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/china/guangdong.html), snapshot `guangdong-260923.osm.pbf` (data through `2026-09-23T20:22:04Z`). Uses the mapped `natural=coastline` ways, including airport reclamation, harbour quays, Deep Bay and outlying islands; small offshore polygons below 0.5 SVG square units are omitted for legibility.
- Hong Kong/Shenzhen land colours: [Hong Kong administrative boundary, OSM relation 913110](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/913110). The visible border river uses the mapped water polygon [relation 9791660](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9791660), rather than an invented gap between the land shapes.
- Registration: WGS84 coordinates fitted to the existing map using modern East Rail, Tsuen Wan, Tung Chung and Tuen Ma station control points. Coastlines were simplified with a topology-preserving tolerance of 0.25 SVG units, without moving railway paths or stations. This improves the background's geographic accuracy within the original map's approximate projection; it is not a survey. The background shows **present-day geography throughout playback**, not historical reclamation stages.

- Sha Tau Kok and early KCR: museum booklet and annual reports above. Historic curves and station positions remain approximate; a date citation does not certify their coordinates.
- Modern geographic cross-checks: [East Rail](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/4248589), [Tsuen Wan](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/269669), [Tung Chung](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/5317704), [Tuen Ma](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/6102298), [XRL](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9405634).
- The XRL geometry was corrected through Kwai Chung/Shek Kong using mapped track plus the LegCo alignment. It continues into Shenzhen at the SVG boundary; only Hong Kong mileage is counted. Old Beacon Hill and Tsim Sha Tsui approaches are historical reconstructions, not current OSM railway.
- Light Rail is simplified. The documented allocation is 36.2 km today, with 4.4 km for 2003 extensions, 3.2 km for earlier Tin Shui Wai track and 28.6 km for the older Tuen Mun/Yuen Long area. Splits within that last group were prorated by drawn length: **estimates, not measured historical engineering lengths**.
- Airport Express and the Tung Chung line share one pair of tracks west of Tsing Yi, across the Tsing Ma Bridge to Lantau; Airport Express passes through Sunny Bay on the centre tracks ([Tung Chung line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tung_Chung_line), [Sunny Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Bay_station)). The map draws the two lines side by side instead of the dashed Airport Express overlay on the Tung Chung centreline it used on Lantau and from Kowloon to Hong Kong. On the shared track they touch (`0.95 W`, like Shanghai's Lines 3/4), with Airport Express on the north side on Lantau; they part to `2 W` round Sunny Bay and from Tsing Yi to Hong Kong, where Tung Chung-only stations need the clearance. Airport Express crosses to the south side just after Sunny Bay, where the tracks really divide (it runs through the station's centre tracks). On the shared track neither line has a real side, and this one swap avoids crossings with the Disneyland Resort, Tsuen Wan or Tuen Ma lines that would read as interchanges. Its 34.0 km Hong Kong - Airport track and the 1.3 km AsiaWorld-Expo extension give the published 35.3 km.
- Termini end at their station markers. Tails that continued past a terminus were trimmed: Tsuen Wan, Kennedy Town, North Point (Kwun Tong and Tseung Kwan O lines), Tiu Keng Leng, Lok Ma Chau, Wu Kai Sha, LOHAS Park, Chai Wan, Whampoa, Sunny Bay, AsiaWorld-Expo, the 1979–80 Tsim Sha Tsui terminus and the Tung Chung line at both ends. Light Rail branch ends now finish on the centreline of the track they join, so the flat caps leave no notch. The KCR line keeps its end at the Lo Wu boundary bridge (`data-continues`), because the railway continued into China and Lo Wu had no station from 1911 to 1949.

<a id="shanghai"></a>

## Shanghai (`shanghai`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/shanghai/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/shanghai/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/shanghai/map.svg).

Scope: Shanghai Metro, the Shanghai Suburban Railway lines (Jinshan Railway, Airport Link Line) and the Maglev, with the Songjiang trams as tracks only. Station tooltips use `metro`, `suburban` (Jinshan Railway and Airport Link stations) and `maglev`. Maglev stations show Shanghai Maglev Transportation's swoosh (`shanghai-maglev.svg`), cropped from the [public-domain SMT logo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SMT_logo.svg) with its "SMT" lettering removed and the viewBox padded top and bottom so the wide swoosh matches the other logos' visual weight at tooltip height. Pudong Airport shows only the Maglev symbol until Line 2 arrives on 2010-04-08. The first public days of Line 1 are an open question under the spec §7 opening rule (accuracy gap 2 and the 1993-05-28 row). The Maglev appears on 2003-01-01 with weekend sightseeing round trips and stays on the map through the 2003-03-10 – 2003-09-19 pause (software upgrade, then SARS; spec §7 draws no gap), and its airport opening (2003-10-11), daily trial operation (2003-12-29) and commercial operation (2006-04-27) are separate events.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Timeline of Shanghai Metro][p-sh-timeline] — **Recovered**. User-specified completeness checklist; secondary, not final authority where dates conflict. Includes renames, transfers and temporary closures beyond this build-history scope.
- [Minhang government account: thirty years of Shanghai Metro][p-sh-early] — **New**. Line 1 historical opening stages; government-authored retrospective hosted by The Paper.
- [Shanghai government: South Railway Station and Xinzhuang opening][p-sh-xinzhuang] — **New**. Xinzhuang's first Jinshan Railway passenger train on 5 January 2025; do not confuse the mainline high-speed upgrade with a new metro line.
- [Shanghai government / Jinshan district: 1·5 timetable change][p-sh-jinshan-timetable] — **New**. Dated timetable and fare-map images for Jinshan services from 5 January 2025.
- [Shanghai Basic Facts 2024][p-sh-statistics] — **New**. Government network statistics and geographic context; aggregate length only, not a source for each SVG segment.
- [Shanghai Release: Jinghong Road temporary underground passage][p-sh-jinghong-open] — **New**. Operator announcement reproduced by Shanghai Release/Sina: 5 July 2025 opening and unchanged fare system.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Exact upstream SVG revision/author has not been recovered. Existing rivers and the original metro alignments are inherited illustration; the Shanghai timeline is a history source, not geographic evidence.

- [Songjiang Tram 1](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/14251681), [Tram 2](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/16159672) and [Line 9](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/214629) were recovered as alignment cross-checks. T2’s old Canghua spur uses the current T1 alignment as geometric context; historical service still needs the dated route description.
- Songjiang University Town’s short branch and local offsets at Sports Center depict simplified tram connections. They must not be read as survey-accurate co-location.
- Shanghai Railway Station, West Nanjing Road, Caoyang Road and other walking transfers need separate paid-area identities. A shared name or fare concession does not justify merging all markers or highlighting every line’s platforms.
- The early Jinjiang Park/Shanghai South and Zhangjiang High-Tech Park replacement alignments require historical maps. Modern line geometry cannot independently verify removed surface stations.

<a id="taipei"></a>

## Taipei (`taipei`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/taipei/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/taipei/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/taipei/map.svg).

Scope follows [Taipei Metro's official route map](https://web.metro.taipei/pages/assets/images/routemap2026-en.png), which draws New Taipei Metro's Circular, Sanying, Danhai and Ankeng lines and the Taoyuan Airport MRT as part of the network (spec §8). Danhai and Ankeng are light rail, drawn as tracks only; Hongshulin and Shisizhang list them in `data-lines` from their openings. Taipei Metro operated the Circular Line from its opening until 2023-05-22; from 2023-05-23 its stations show New Taipei Metro ([Wikipedia](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_line_(New_Taipei_Metro)>); registered to New Taipei on 2023-01-31, physically handed over on 2023-05-23 per [zh 新北捷運](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/新北捷運)), using the text-free symbol from [its Chinese Wikipedia logo file](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_Taipei_Metro_logo.svg) with editor metadata removed. That file is marked non-free (a trademark used under fair use); no free text-free version was found. Airport MRT stations show Taoyuan Metro's symbol, `taoyuan-metro.svg`, from [File:Taoyuan Metro logo plain.svg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taoyuan_Metro_logo_plain.svg). That file is tagged PD-ineligible (US only; Taiwan) and trademarked, and its colours match the [operator's own logo](https://www.tymetro.com.tw/tymetro-new/_images/all/logo.png). Editor metadata and nested transforms were flattened, and it contains no lettering.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Taipei Metro: Chronicles][p-tp-official] — **New**. Operator opening chronology and section lengths. Use the dated entries, not a later line name applied retrospectively.
- [Taipei Metro: 大事紀][p-tp-chronicles-zh] — **New**. Native-language operator chronology; cross-check opening/renaming wording against English translations.
- [Taipei Metro annual report 2015][p-tp-report-2015] — **New**. Operational route-name convention and Dingpu opening. Naming announcements and earlier through-service changes are not necessarily the same date.
- [Taipei Metro annual report 2007][p-tp-report-2007] — **New**. Historical sections and lengths; use to reconcile SVG kilometres instead of measuring the drawing.
- [Maokong Gondola: Chronicles][p-tp-gondola-history] — **Recovered**. Passenger opening 4 July 2007; later temporary suspensions are operational history, not demolition.
- [Maokong Gondola: system introduction][p-tp-gondola-profile] — **Recovered**. 4.03 km, four passenger stations and two angle stations. Only passenger stations contribute to the map count.
- [Maokong Gondola: transport connections][p-tp-gondola-access] — **Recovered**. Taipei Zoo MRT–gondola walking connection, approximately 350 m; not one paid-area station.
- [Taipei Metro route map 2026 (English)](https://web.metro.taipei/pages/assets/images/routemap2026-en.png) — **New**. Scope source (spec §8) and badge colours for LB, V and K.
- [New Taipei City: Sanying Line opens 30 June](https://www.ntpc.gov.tw/ch/home.jsp?id=e8ca970cde5c00e1&dataserno=9eddd1f8da661071318da507f2acbc87) — **New**. Official opening at 14:00 on 2026-06-30; trial operation, fare-free, until 31 August ([hours extended, CNA](https://www.cna.com.tw/news/aloc/202607300233.aspx)); fares from 1 September.
- [NTMC: Ankeng LRT opens 10 February](https://www.ntmetro.com.tw/basic/?mode=detail&node=578) — **New**. Opening ceremony in the morning, first public train 13:00 the same day; free trial operation to 12 March ([Focus Taiwan](https://focustaiwan.tw/society/202302100016)).
- [CNA: Blue Coast Line opens 15 November 2020](https://www.cna.com.tw/news/firstnews/202011140019.aspx) — **New**. Fare-free until 14 December; first-day riders reported by [TVBS](https://news.tvbs.com.tw/life/1417251).
- [Taipei Times: Danhai LRT first section opens](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/archives/2018/12/24/2003706693) — **New**. Ceremony 23 December 2018, public service from 24 December ([Taiwan News](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/3601751)).
- [China Post: Airport MRT begins commercial operations (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/20170302095929/http://www.chinapost.com.tw/taiwan/national/national-news/2017/03/02/492718/Airport-MRT.htm) — **New**. 2 March 2017. Invited group rides from 2 February (government bodies and the rail industry, not counted), then free public trial rides with 20,000 numbered tickets a day, 8:00–16:00, from 16 February: the date used (spec §7).
- [CNA: Laojie River station opens 31 July 2023](https://www.cna.com.tw/news/ahel/202307270118.aspx) — **New**. Opened to passengers at 11:50 ([Taoyuan Metro notice](https://www.tymetro.com.tw/tymetro-new/tw/_pages/news/show-1822-1.html)).
- [Taoyuan Metro: A1 Taipei Main Station transfers](https://www.tymetro.com.tw/tymetro-new/tw/_pages/travel-guide/A1) — **New**. Walking transfers (10–15 min) to Taipei Metro Taipei Main Station and Beimen; drawn as out-of-station connectors.
- [LTN: Sanying Dingpu transfer](https://news.ltn.com.tw/news/life/breakingnews/5249474) — **New**. Tap out of the Bannan Line, tap in to the Sanying Line: an out-of-station transfer (connector from 2026-06-30).

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Exact upstream SVG revision/author has not been recovered. The pre-existing metro map provides the base geography; sources for openings are independent of that artwork.

- [Xiaobitan branch](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/4250381) and [Songshan–Xindian](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/4250357) underpin the branch correction: continue roughly south with the main line from Qizhang before bending west.
- [Maokong Gondola track way 71266575](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/71266575) and [route relation 17787820](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/17787820) supply the added cable alignment and four passenger stops. Intermediate angle facilities influence the route but are not passenger markers.
- The operator specifies a walk from Taipei Zoo MRT to the gondola. Banqiao/Circular Line and Xinpu/Xinpu Minsheng similarly need separate identities, not automatic grouping by proximity/name.
- Compare stored section lengths against operator historical tables: for example the operator chronology quotes 10.5 km for the initial Muzha section and 8.4 km for the Guting–Xindian extension, whereas existing allocations use different totals. These require reconciliation, not a blanket “verified” label.
- The four added lines follow OSM route relations ([Airport MRT 2108764](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/2108764), [Sanying 21066080](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/21066080), [Danhai 9154523](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9154523) / [Blue Coast 13611116](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13611116), [Ankeng 15443525](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/15443525); Geofabrik Taiwan 2026-09-23, © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0). They are projected through the existing Taipei affine fit, with a Gaussian local correction from the matched stations near the existing network, and drawn as smooth Béziers with stations as forced vertices. Local offsets of at most 8 units keep the Airport MRT clear of Beimen and New Taipei Industrial Park (Circular Line), and Sanying's Dingpu beside, not on, the Bannan terminus.
- North of Hongshulin the Danhai LRT runs beside the Tamsui–Xinyi Line for about 0.3 km (OSM tracks 1–2 map units apart); it is drawn as a parallel offset 4.5 units away on its diverging side, starting from Hongshulin's marker centre, so both colours stay visible.
- Separate identities: `station-taipei-main-station-a1`, `station-sanchong-a2`, `station-new-taipei-industrial-park-a3` and `station-dingpu-lb01` are separate stations from their Taipei Metro namesakes (out-of-station connectors).
- Canvas re-extended on 2026-09-26 to `-6916 -1589 13513 8393` so the Airport MRT fits between the panels (the extra legend pills also make the legend taller). The ring outside the previous frame uses the same OSM snapshot, fit and thresholds as the earlier expansion. It adds 頭前溪, 鳳山溪, Shimen Reservoir and 寶山第二水庫, and shades Taipei, New Taipei and Taoyuan as the operator's land. Geography inside the previous frame is unchanged, except that fills are merged across the seam and hairline strokes on the old frame edges are removed. `initialBounds`/`initialView` are unchanged, and opening transforms were verified identical at five laptop sizes and on mobile.

## Singapore (`singapore`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/singapore/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/singapore/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/singapore/map.svg).

### Primary records and other focused references

- [LTA: Rail Network][p-sg-network] — **New**. Official network map, line inventory, names and interchanges; current layout does not establish historic opening dates.
- [LTA: Downtown Line][p-sg-dtl] — **New**. Stages 1–3, Hume opening and published lengths; distinguish complete project lengths from operating sections.
- [LTA: Thomson-East Coast Line][p-sg-tel] — **New**. Opening stages, deferred stations and planned extensions; lists Stage 4 opening 23 June 2024.
- [LTA: Sengkang–Punggol LRT][p-sg-splrt] — **New**. Network layout and system-level opening years, not every later infill station day.
- [SBS Transit: Ridership][p-sg-sbs] — **New**. Operator states Sengkang LRT opened 18 January 2003 and Punggol LRT 29 January 2005.
- [National Library Board: Woodlands MRT station][p-sg-woodlands] — **New**. Historical account with primary newspaper and government references for the Woodlands extension.
- [SMRT operations review 2020: milestones][p-sg-smrt] — **New**. Operator historical milestones; useful corroboration of early network stages, not every exact date.
- [LTA: Punggol Coast to open for passenger service][p-sg-punggol] — **New**. 10 December 2024 opening and North East Line extension.
- [LTA: Circle Line 6][p-sg-ccl6] — **New**. Three new stations, closed loop, passenger opening 12 July 2026; links the separate 4 July preview notice (the preview is the date used for the new stations, spec §7).
- [LTA newsroom: Circle Line 6 notices][p-sg-ccl6-preview] — **New**. 14 May 2026 notice explicitly distinguishes 4 July public preview from 12 July passenger service; exact article should replace this index link when available.
- [LTA annual report 2024/25][p-sg-report-2025] — **New**. Recent network milestones, including Teck Lee LRT opening; simplified LRT markers intentionally omit most intermediate stops.

### Line and station inventory

Each history below includes a route/station table and references for intermediate station names and openings, supplementing the event prose. These are **secondary sources unless explicitly labelled as operator/government records above**. “SVG km now” is the current stored sum on the review date, shown for reconciliation—not a newly verified length. `0.0` on a predecessor means it has no active track today.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Exact upstream SVG revision/author has not been recovered. LTA’s official network maps substantiate station names and connectivity, but they are schematic and do not independently certify geographic Bézier coordinates. A complete geographic retrace of the inherited Singapore SVG has **not** been established by the recovered research.

- Use LTA’s line pages for operating length and stage maps, plus the station tables below for opening chronology. Do not count planned TEL stations merely because they appear on a project map.
- Bukit Panjang, Sengkang and Punggol LRT are marked `simplified` in the legend and use simplified track coverage. Intermediate stop openings are not all separate markers/events; this is a scope choice, not evidence those stops never existed.
- Document line-total rounding and branch accounting before treating section `data-km` as precise engineering measurements. The completed Circle Line’s ring and Marina Bay spur need consistent treatment.
- Cartographic adjustment (present before the 2026-09-26 audit): around Outram Park, Chinatown and Tanjong Pagar the East–West, North East, Circle, Downtown and Thomson–East Coast tracks were re-routed locally, seven circles moved (Chinatown by about 16 units) and the Outram Park capsules made more compact. Dates, `data-lines` and `data-km` are unchanged; it is a drawing change, not a relocation.

<a id="tokyo"></a>

## Tokyo — Metro / Toei (`tokyo`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/tokyo/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/tokyo/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/tokyo/map.svg).

Scope: Tokyo Metro and Toei and their predecessors, including Toei's Toden Arakawa Line and Nippori–Toneri Liner (both tracks only); JR and private railways appear on the subway map only as connections and are excluded (spec §8). The Arakawa Line's Oji Electric Tramway predecessor starts the timeline on 1911-08-20, so the slider starts in 1911. The header shows both the Tokyo Metro and Toei logos; station tooltips use `metro` and `toei` (alt text "Toei", also used for Toden and Liner stops). Eidan's 2004 corporatisation as Tokyo Metro is a rename, not a handover, and is not modelled (spec §5).

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Tokyo Metro: corporate history (Japanese)][p-ty-metro-history] — **New**. Primary opening milestones and corporate chronology; company establishment 4 July 1941 is distinct from operating takeover 1 September.
- [Tokyo Metro: corporate history (English)][p-ty-metro-en] — **New**. English cross-check for principal openings and English line nomenclature.
- [Toei: subway history][p-ty-toei] — **New**. Detailed primary chronology for all four Toei lines, extensions, line names and station renames.
- [Toei Asakusa Line 60th anniversary][p-ty-asakusa60] — **New**. Historical opening stages and station names, supplementing the operator chronology.
- [Tokyo Metro corporate profile][p-ty-profile] — **New**. Current station counts and operating lengths; branch/shared-track accounting requires care.
- [Toei business plan 2025: current network][p-ty-toei-profile] — **New**. Operator line lengths and station inventory; not historical segment measurements.
- [Tokyo Metro: historical Ginza platforms][p-ty-platforms] — **Recovered**. Original Ginza Line platform context; supports historical arrangement, not exact coordinates of every drawn old platform.
- [Tokyo Metro: Shibuya station relocation plan][p-ty-shibuya] — **Recovered**. 2020 Ginza platform relocation and station layout.
- [Toei: Toden Arakawa Line history][p-ty-toden-ayumi] — **New**. Operator chronology: Oji Electric Tramway's 1911-08-20 Asukayama-ue – Otsuka opening, full route 1930-03-30, 1942-02-01 integration into Tokyo City, routes 27/32 combined and renamed Arakawa Line 1974-10-01, nickname 2017-04-28.
- [Toei: Nippori–Toneri Liner history][p-ty-nt-ayumi] — **New**. Opening 2008-03-30 (Nippori – Minumadai-shinsuikoen).
- [Toei: Liner opening date announced (2007)][p-ty-nt-open] — **New**. Press release fixing the 30 March 2008 opening.
- [Toei: Arakawa Line nickname decided (2017-04-28)][p-ty-sakura] — **New**. Japanese 東京さくらトラム, English "Tokyo Sakura Tram", to be used from the announcement.
- [Toei: Toden stop pages][p-ty-toden-stops] and [Toei: Liner station pages][p-ty-nt-stops] — **New**. The "乗換え案内" section of each page is the transfer test for §8: Minowabashi (Minowa), Machiya-ekimae (Machiya), Oji-ekimae (Oji), Shin-koshinzuka (Nishi-sugamo), Higashi-ikebukuro-yonchome (Higashi-ikebukuro), Kishibojimmae (Zoshigaya) and Liner Nishi-nippori (Chiyoda Line). Toden-Zoshigaya, Waseda and Otsuka-ekimae list no Metro/Toei transfer.

Toei's subway chronology records line names only on 1978-07-01 (Lines 1, 6 and 10 become Asakusa, Mita and Shinjuku) and 2000-04-20 (Line 12 becomes Oedo). The earlier "Toei Asakusa/Mita/Shinjuku Line → Asakusa/Mita/Shinjuku Line" renames on 2000-04-20 had no source and were removed on 2026-09-26; the unprefixed names match Toei's English line list and the Tokyo Metro names.

The Arakawa Line had no line name before 1974. Following the Ginza Line's "Tokyo Underground Railway → Eidan Subway" precedent, its legend names the operator of each period: Oji Electric Tramway (to 1942-02-01), Tokyo City Tram (to 1943-07-01, the metropolis system) and Toden (to 1974-10-01). Toden route numbers 27 (Minowabashi–Akabane) and 32 (Arakawa-shakomae–Waseda) are not used as names, because their start dates are unverified and both ran over Arakawa-shakomae–Oji-ekimae. The 2017-04-28 nickname "Tokyo Sakura Tram" is treated as a rename, like Oshiage (SKYTREE).

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Recovered original artwork: [Tokyo Subway Linemap en.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tokyo_Subway_Linemap_en.svg), Yveltal, CC BY-SA 4.0; the source used was the June 2020 map. Keep its file-history attribution rather than substituting a similarly named Tokyo map. Only Tokyo Metro/Toei and their predecessors are in scope; faded private/JR connecting railways in the supplied map were excluded.

- Recovered alignment comparisons: [Ginza](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/8026074), [Yurakucho](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/443269), [Fukutoshin](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/5375678), [Hanzomon](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/443279), [Namboku](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/7730199), [Mita](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/443286), [Oedo](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/3355612).
- Smoothing and shorter interchange symbols intentionally move local control points/markers slightly. These are cartographic edits, not track relocation events. The latest pass (present before the 2026-09-26 audit) smoothed 26 central track sections around Otemachi, Kasumigaseki, Hibiya, Toranomon, Shimbashi, Mitsukoshimae and Nihombashi, moved 17 circles by up to about 3 units and shortened or re-angled 8 capsules; its four walking connectors were then straightened back to single segments (spec §5). Dates and `data-km` are unchanged. Modern OSM cannot prove historic Manseibashi, Shimbashi, Omotesando or pre-2020 Shibuya platform coordinates.
- Use the operator’s historical-platform and Shibuya-relocation plans above, plus the station-specific histories below, to distinguish these real relocations from drawing adjustments.
- Namboku/Mita shared track and Marunouchi/Ogikubo predecessor accounting need line-specific length definitions; summing advertised line lengths can double-count physical track.
- Toden Arakawa Line and the Nippori–Toneri Liner (added 2026-09-26) are simplified lines (§8): tracks only, 0.4 W. Their geometry comes from OpenStreetMap route relations [9254425](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9254425) and [3423146](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/3423146) (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; API snapshot 2026-09-26), projected with the retained Tokyo WGS84→SVG affine and simplified at 0.15 units. Each line is displaced locally, with a Gaussian taper, to pass through the designated heavy-rail marker: Minowa 20 units (the tram terminus is drawn at Minowa, not at Minowabashi), Nishi-sugamo 19.5, Oji 11 and at most 6 elsewhere. Where the schematic Fukutoshin and Namboku drawings overlap the tram, it is offset 3.6 units. The section kilometres come from the stop-distance table and sum to Toei's 12.2 km and 9.7 km. The wartime suspension of 1944 to 1946-07-10 is omitted under §7. The 1925–28 split stops at Otsuka and the 1915 Oji terminus south of the main line are below drawing scale.
- The Liner's northern end (y ≈ −105) lies above the original opening frame but inside the viewBox.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Recovered original artwork: [Shenzhen Metro (Rapid Transit) System Map.svg](<https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Shenzhen_Metro_(Rapid_Transit)_System_Map.svg>), Wahsaw, CC BY-SA 4.0. Its revision predates some additions. Geography for later lines was supplemented with mapped track and station coordinates, not inferred solely from a current schematic.

- Added/revised alignments: [Line 3](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/2287559), [Line 6 Branch](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/14953716), [Line 7](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/6781618), [Line 8](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13176926), [Line 12](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/14944728), [Line 13](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/18470804), [Line 16](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/15059917).
- Additional cross-checks: [Line 5](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/2752389), [Line 11](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9318441). Small offsets remain around separate paid-area markers; a smooth curve is not a surveyed centreline.
- Longhua Tram and Pingshan Skyshuttle are simplified. The Skyshuttle drawing was deliberately adjusted to reach the selected metro interchange markers, like the existing Guanlan representation. This is **not evidence that the actual tracks pass through those metro platforms**. Real walking/paid-area arrangements must be taken from station plans.
- Use the Line 13 engineering report above for an independent alignment cross-check; future planned connections shown there are not historical service.
- Operators: stations show `metro` (Shenzhen Metro) or `mtr` (MTR Shenzhen). Line 4's first section switches on the 2010-07-01 handover, which has its own event; its later sections and all of Line 13 show MTR from opening (spec §5).
- Cartographic adjustment (present before the 2026-09-26 audit): the short Yinhu capsule (Lines 6/9, from 2020-08-18) is rotated from 34.8° to −50.5° to follow the shared Line 6/9 corridor (spec §5). Its position and dates are unchanged.

## Hangzhou (`hangzhou`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/hangzhou/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/hangzhou/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/hangzhou/map.svg).

Scope: Hangzhou Metro. Hanghai Intercity and Shaoxing Line 1 appear on the official map only as connections and are excluded (spec §8).

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Hangzhou news: Line 1 public rides, 19 November 2012][p-hz-preview1] — **New**. Free public trial rides (免费试乘) 18–21 November 2012, the first public riding and the date used under the spec §7; ticketed trial operation followed on 24 November.
- [Central government: Hangzhou Metro opens, 24 November 2012][p-hz-regular1] — **New**. Regular service date, named in the 18 November event.
- [Zhejiang Online: Line 1 ticketed trial operation from 24 November, 14:30](http://zjnews.zjol.com.cn/05zjnews/system/2012/11/23/018965441.shtml) — **New**.
- [Hangzhou news: Line 2 south-east section opens for trial operation, 24 November 2014](https://hznews.hangzhou.com.cn/chengshi/content/2014-11/24/content_5538094_0.htm) — **New**.
- [Hangzhou news: Line 2 trial rides, 17 November 2014][p-hz-preview2] — **New**. Free trial rides 18–22 November 2014 (the date used); regular service 24 November.
- [Hangzhou news: East Railway Station transfer guide][p-hz-east-square] — **New**. 6 November 2021 Line 6 opening and separate East Square paid area.
- [Hangzhou Metro release: Shentangqiao passage opens tomorrow][p-hz-shentang-open] — **New**. Operator-authored notice reproduced by Hangzhou news: paid-area passage opens 1 November 2022.
- [Hangzhou government: 2021 station-name approval][p-hz-name-approval] — **New**. Approval of names; does not alone establish the later 26 January 2022 passenger-signage change.
- [Government account: Zhijiang Culture Center station rename][p-hz-zhijiang-name] — **New**. Effective 1 February 2024, formerly Zhipu Road.
- [Hangzhou news: Jingchang Road opening][p-hz-jingchang] — **New**. Announces 30 June 2025 infill opening.
- [Hangzhou environmental authority: airport express engineering report][p-hz-19-plan] — **Recovered**. Route and station geography for Line 19; distinguish approved alignment from operating history.
- [Zhejiang Online / Qianjiang Evening News: two station renames][p-hz-renames-2022] — **New**. Reports operator confirmation: Dongxinyuan and Linpingnan names take effect on 26 January 2022.
- [China Association of Metros: 2025 operating-line statistics][p-gz-camet] also covers the 2025 Hangzhou Line 5 extension.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

The supplied Hangzhou SVG is the geographic base, but its exact upstream artwork URL/revision has not been recovered. Do not attribute it to an unrelated Commons schematic. Later additions were checked against station coordinates and mapped track, supplemented by the airport express engineering report.

- Reconstructed/corrected corridors: [Line 3 main](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13538220), [Shima branch](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/14280625), [Line 5](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/10386952), [Line 7](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13061278), [Line 9](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13060896), [Line 19](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/14613131).
- [Line 1](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/4627560) and [Line 10](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13535687) were comparison alignments. The later audit corrected Gudang Xincun, Yicheng Road and Pinglan Road positions while retaining compact interchange offsets.
- East Railway Station and East Square remain separate paid areas even after eligible tickets gain continuous fares. Shentangqiao’s actual passage opening has its own 1 November 2022 source.
- Unopened Tiaoxi and deferred intermediate platforms must not be inferred open from the full planned project length. Verify operating extent before using a line-total kilometre figure.

<a id="guangfo"></a>

## Guangzhou / Foshan (`guangfo`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/guangfo/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/guangfo/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/guangfo/map.svg).

Scope: the Guangzhou and Foshan metro networks together, with the APM and the Haizhu, Huangpu and Nanhai trams (trams as tracks only). Guangzhou's intercity railways appear on the official map only as connections and are excluded (spec §8). The header shows both the Guangzhou Metro and Foshan Metro logos, and station tooltips use `guangzhou` and `foshan`.

### Primary records and other focused references

- [China Association of Metros: 2025 operating-line statistics][p-gz-camet] — **New**. Industry statistical table: opening dates, operating lengths and station counts, including GZ 10/12 and Huangpu Tram 2, and Hangzhou Line 5 extension.
- [Southcn: Chigang Line 12 opening][p-gz-chigang] — **New**. 13 February 2026 opening of previously bypassed Line 12 platforms.
- [Southcn: Foshan Line 3 through operation][p-gz-f3-through] — **New**. Reports Foshan rail authority approval: 18 June 2026 full connection. Need separate evidence for deferred Foshan Railway Station.
- [China News Service: Foshan hub opening][p-gz-foshan-station] — **New**. 1 July 2026 railway/metro station opening, distinct from 18 June through running.
- [Guangdong Transport Department: Nanhai Tram extension][p-gz-nanhai-open] — **New**. 29 November 2022 extension; retrospectively confirms 18 August 2021 initial opening; Linyuexi same-platform transfer without leaving the paid area.
- [Guangzhou government: South Railway Station paid-area passage][p-gz-south-transfer] — **New**. 21 January 2024, linking Foshan Line 2 to Guangzhou Lines 2, 7 and 22.

| 2014-12-31 | Haizhu Tram: Canton Tower - Wanshengwei paid trial-ride period begins                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | [Nanfang Daily via People's Daily, 30 December 2014](http://cpc.people.com.cn/n/2014/1230/c87228-26296628.html). It gives the 开通试乘期 from 31 December 2014 to 11 February 2015 as daily service from 9:00 to 17:00 at a 13-minute headway, with first and last trains posted at stations and a 2-yuan day ticket ("试乘纪念券…当天可多次试乘") on sale at every station. From 12 February service moved to 试运营 with 羊城通 and single-journey tickets. Also: [Haizhu district page](https://www.haizhu.gov.cn/hzdt/ztlm/tzhz/rjhj/lyjd/csmp/content/post_9173297.html) "2014年12月31日正式开通试运营"; [Bendibao, 3 February 2015](http://jt.gz.bendibao.com/news/201523/180533.shtml); [Haizhu Tram][gz-tram]. **Note (spec §7):** despite the "试乘" (trial ride) label, the opening period was paid public service on a timetable, not a free trial-ride promotion, so it counts. From 12 February 2015 the line moved to 全线试运营 (regular service), recorded as its own event. Pati (Beer Museum) did not open with the line; the simplified tram draws no stop markers.                                                                                                                                 |

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

Recovered base artwork: [Guangzhou Metro Map en.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Guangzhou_Metro_Map_en.svg), ASDFGH, CC BY-SA 3.0. The user-supplied `og.svg` preserved Foshan geometry; `ref.svg` was a later network cross-check, not a replacement for geographic alignment. Those input filenames alone are not durable external citations.

- Modern additions/corrections: [Line 3](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9841062), [5](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/7483883), [7](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/7520751), [10](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/19283541), [11](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/18132492), [12 east](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/19283546), [12 west](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/19283549), [13](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/6728313), [14](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/8338723), [22](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13987999), [Huangpu Tram 2](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/19382702).
- Restored/extended Foshan corridors: [Line 2](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13604443), [Line 3](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/15054264), [Nanhai Tram](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/13103097). Use dated notices for which part of these modern routes was open at each event.
- Ersha Island and other added stations were recalibrated against geographic coordinates. Chinese map coordinates may be GCJ-02 while OSM is WGS84; mixing them shifts stations systematically. Bézier smoothing and compact interchange offsets remain presentation adjustments.
- Western canvas/rivers were extended using mapped water geometry to avoid clipping inherited rivers. That edit is a present-day background repair, not a history of land reclamation or river changes.
- Nanhai’s Linyuexi paid-area transfer is explicitly supported by the Guangdong Transport Department notice. APM/metro and several tram walking links must not be assumed to share paid areas merely because a passage exists.

## Chengdu (`chengdu`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/chengdu/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/chengdu/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/chengdu/map.svg).

### Primary records and other focused references

- [Chengdu Metro app API: station list][p-cd-chengdu-metro-app-api-station-list] — **New**. Every line, official English station name and transfer line; the live copy of 2026-09-24 was compared with an archived copy of 2024-07-10. The transfer lists are the test for designated interchanges (§6).
- [Chengdu Rail Transit: English station list (archived 2017–2023)][p-cd-chengdu-rail-transit-english-station-lis] — **New**. Pre-2023 English station names; more than 70 captures from 2017-12-08 to 2023-01-05.
- [Official network map, February 2023 (archived)][p-cd-official-network-map-february-2023-archi] — **New**. Pre-revision English names; the December 2024 and December 2025 editions show the post-July-2023 names, Line S3 and Tram Line 2.
- [Sichuan Online, 2025-09-16][p-cd-sichuan-online-2025-09-16] and [China News Service, 2025-12-05][p-cd-china-news-service-2025-12-05] — **New**. Operator figures for Line 17 phase 2, Line 13 and Line 30 (lengths, stations, first public day).
- [Red Star News via Sina, 2026-09-24][p-cd-red-star-news-via-sina-2026-09-24] — **New**. Announces the Line 2 east section's return on 2026-09-28 on its new alignment.
- [Wikimedia Commons: Chengdu Rail Transit icon][p-cd-wikimedia-commons-chengdu-rail-transit-i] — **New**. Source of the logo; public domain as a text logo, with a trademark notice. The app preserves the complete mark’s shapes and proportions, with its original blue fills and no added background.
- Each event row below cites the notices and reports behind that date; station lists and English names otherwise follow the operator app and the archived English station list.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

- **Artwork.** The supplied SVG is an Illustrator export of a geographic Chengdu Metro map (roughly the mid-2024 network: it has Qingdao Road but not Line 27 or the Line 8 phase 2 extensions). Its upstream source and licence are not recorded. Lines are outlined strokes; their centrelines were recovered exactly from the two sides of each ribbon (§12). Stripe-drawn shared stretches (Lines 5/6 at Xibei Bridge, 18/19 to the airport) were rebuilt as full-width parallels, and Line 1’s doubly drawn trunk at Sihe as one track with the Wugensong branch leaving it.
- **Added lines.** Lines 13, 27, 30 and S3 and the extensions of Lines 8, 10 and 17 follow OpenStreetMap route relations ([OSM: Line 13][cd-osm-line-13], [OSM: Line 27][cd-osm-line-27], [OSM: Line 30][cd-osm-line-30], [OSM: Line S3][cd-osm-line-s3], [OSM: Line 8][cd-osm-line-8], [OSM: Line 10][cd-osm-line-10], [OSM: Line 17][cd-osm-line-17]), retrieved 2026-09-24. Coordinates were fitted to the artwork with an affine transform on 20 line termini, then a Gaussian local correction from 329 matched stations (median residual 1.1 units, about 20 m).
- **Water and outside land.** Water is the union of OpenStreetMap `natural=water`, `waterway=riverbank` and `landuse=reservoir` areas retrieved 2026-09-24, through the same fit; ponds under 60 square units are dropped and outlines simplified at 0.4 units. Land outside [OSM: Chengdu municipality boundary][cd-osm-chengdu-municipality-boundary] is tinted. The background is present-day geography throughout playback.
- **Western extent.** The frame extends 1,552.494 units westward to put Tianfu Square at its horizontal midpoint. All original coordinates shift right by that amount; track shapes, station alignment and scale are unchanged. The added western water areas use the same geographic fit and 2026-09-24 OpenStreetMap data, with the municipality boundary extended across the new frame.
- **Placement exceptions.** Line 10’s Terminal 2 of Shuangliu International Airport is moved 14 units along its track so the out-of-station pair with East of Terminal 2 reads as two stations (2.4 r). Line 30’s Financial City North is moved 4.5 units clear of Line 18. At the airport, Lines 10 and 19 run in parallel closer than the marker clearance (tolerated shared corridor, §5).
- **Tram.** Chengdu Tram Line 2 is drawn as simplified track; its metro interchanges shown in `data-lines` are the same-named Chengdu West Railway Station (from 2019-12-27), Tianhe Road (2019-12-27) and Wangcong Temple (2020-12-18, when Line 6 opened). The official map also marks Xipu Campus ↔ Xingye North Street and Longyin ↔ Zitonggong; they are not included (different names, no dated designation).
- **Kilometres.** Published line totals (China Association of Metros 2024 and operator releases) govern: Line 18’s 69.39 km is split by drawn length because its published 55.95 km first section conflicts with station spacing (≈48.2 km); Line 3’s phases 2 and 3 and Line 4’s 2017 extensions share their published remainder by drawn length; Line 19 counts the shared Line 18 track from Tianfu Station at Line 18’s own allocation (total 99.7 km; the operator says over 100 km).
- **Colours.** The artwork’s colours are Pantone values (Line 1 Blue 072 C, Line 2 171 C, Line 7 310 C, Line 10 293 C, Line 17 352 C, Line 18 3165 C, Line 19 2718 C) and are kept; Lines 13 and 27 use OpenStreetMap’s values in the same family (103 C, 299 C). The operator app uses a separate screen palette.

<a id="beijing"></a>

## Beijing (`beijing`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/beijing/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/beijing/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/beijing/map.svg).

New map and research, **24 September 2026**. Public passenger history begins on **15 January 1971**, when trial operation began with tickets sold against work-unit letters; restricted-access service counts under the spec §7 opening rule. The 1969 inauguration and the military tracks are not public openings. Includes the subway, Capital and Daxing airport railways, S1, and Xijiao / Yizhuang T1 as simplified tracks. The last recorded change is **30 June 2026** (Tongyun Men); the present-day review also includes the May 2026 Pingguoyuan interchange. Temporary suspensions do not erase built infrastructure. National/suburban rail, construction projects and never-opened platforms are outside scope.

### Primary records and focused references

- **Early openings:** [Beijing Transport Vocational College’s historical account](https://www.bjjt.edu.cn/info/2005/19929.htm) records 1971-01-15, **1971-08-15**, 1971-11-07 and 1973-04-23; August 15 takes precedence over August 5 in the English summary table. The [Beijing Subway chronicle for 1971–1980](https://web.archive.org/web/2013/http://www.bjsubway.com/node/1842) gives the terms. From 1971-01-15 the trial operation had "实行内部售票，接待参观群众。售票办法，凭单位介绍信" (internal ticket sales, visiting groups, tickets only with a work-unit letter). The 1971-08-15 (Yuquan Lu) and 1971-11-07 (Gucheng) extensions ran on the same terms. Then "1972年12月27日，北京地铁由原凭证出售地铁票，改为免证件出售地铁票". Restricted-access service counts under the spec §7 opening rule, so Line 1 opens on the three 1971 dates; the change to sale without papers on 1972-12-27 is recorded as its own event, and so is the formal opening of 15 September 1981 ([北京地铁1号线](https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/北京地铁1号线) "1981年9月15日北京地下铁道一期工程正式验收…地铁一期工程运营线路从苹果园站至北京站区段正式对外开放"; [CCTV, 2021](https://m.news.cctv.com/2021/09/14/ARTIJ7l456BYqiLlhXnnh0hM210914.shtml) "1981年9月15日，全长27.6公里的北京地铁一期工程正式交付运营"). Neither changes the map. The 1971-09-13 – 11-06 and 1973-08-12 – 1974-06-30 war-preparedness stoppages are temporary suspensions (spec §7) and are not drawn. The [municipal history](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/gate/big5/www.beijing.gov.cn/ywdt/gzdt/202410/t20241005_3911383.html) corroborates the 1987 loop reorganization.
- **Line 13 eastern opening:** the [transport commission](https://jtw.beijing.gov.cn/xxgk/xwfbh/201912/t20191209_1007437.html) gives **2003-01-28**, correcting January 9 in some station lists. [Beijing’s construction gazette](https://zjw.beijing.gov.cn/bjjs/gcjs/sznj/zjcg/sz/10934391/2021020215473385426.pdf) covers the 1991–2010 projects.
- **Olympic Sports Center:** [the October 10 contemporary report](https://travel.sina.com.cn/around/2008-10-10/114429534.shtml) says the station first opened on **October 9**, rather than October 10 in the summary chronology. The same report says the whole Olympic branch "昨天(9日)清晨起…开始面向普通乘客开放" (opened to ordinary passengers from the morning of the 9th). Before that it could only be ridden with Olympic tickets or credentials ("乘客需要相关票证才能换乘到这条线上"). Restricted-access service counts under the spec §7 opening rule, so the branch opens on **2008-07-19** (Beitucheng is a Line 8/10 capsule from that day); Olympic Sports Center, which the Olympic service did not serve, opens on 2008-10-09.
- **Xi’erqi relocation:** [December 25, 2010 contemporary report](https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2010-12-25/125121705654.shtml). The new building was north of the old one; reported building separation is not a platform-centre coordinate. The old marker is approximately 260 m south on the mapped railway, not a surveyed historical platform point.
- **Qinghe reroute:** [transport commission construction notice](https://jtw.beijing.gov.cn/xxgk/xwfbh/201912/t20191209_1007592.html) and [February 17 contemporary report](https://news.sina.cn/gn/2019-02-17/detail-ihrfqzka6456088.d.html). The new alignment carried trains from **2019-02-17**; the station itself opened **2019-12-30**, not December 28. Track and station dates are deliberately separate.
- **Fares/transfers:** [2007 unified-fare report](https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2007-10-10/161514056608.shtml), [Dongzhimen’s original 2003 transfer arrangement](https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2003-01-23/0334884481.shtml), [Xizhimen’s transfer history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/西直门站), and the [operator’s current ticket rules](https://www.mtr.bj.cn/page/instructions.html). Airport railways retain separate fares and operators, with internal station-complex capsules under the spec’s cross-system rule. Muxidi and Dazhongsi remain separate stations with connectors.
- **Muxidi:** [municipal transfer explanation](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/sy/jrts/202401/t20240117_3537679.html); a promised future paid-area corridor is not an opened corridor. [Dazhongsi’s station history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/大钟寺站) describes the separate Line 12 / 13 stations.
- **2024 openings:** [municipal opening report](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/ywdt/gzdt/202412/t20241215_3965616.html), covering Lines 3/12 and Changping’s Jimen Qiao extension / Zhufang Bei.
- **2025 delayed stations and extensions:** [Dahong Men, November 8](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/sy/jrts/202511/t20251109_4266635.html); [MTR’s Line 17 middle-section opening release](https://www.mtr.com.hk/archive/corporate/en/press_release/PR-25-094-E.pdf); [Beijing Subway notices](https://www.bjsubway.com/) for Line 18 and Line 6’s Luyang extension on December 27; [the national urban-rail association’s 2025 new-section inventory](https://infosharingp2-oss.camet.org.cn/resources/manual/2026/01/04/759313381470277.pdf).
- **2026:** [Wangjing Xi on Line 17, January 31](https://english.beijing.gov.cn/livinginbeijing/transportation/beijingsubway/202601/t20260131_4480193.html); [Pingguoyuan’s three-line interchange, May 16](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/sy/jrts/202605/t20260516_4653696.html); [Tongyun Men, June 30](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/sy/jrts/202606/t20260629_4737846.html), [confirmed after opening](https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/sy/jrts/202607/t20260701_4741334.html). A closure-only filter would incorrectly discard the new Pingguoyuan transfer: the old Line 1 marker stays drawn, separate from the 6/S1 capsule until May 16.
- **Not open as of the review:** [Fushouling exit-design procurement, September 24](https://ggzyfw.beijing.gov.cn/jyxxggjtbyqs/20260924/5726978.html), [Guangqumenwai Line 17 construction permit](https://ghzrzyw.beijing.gov.cn/zhengwuxinxi/tzgg/dc/202606/t20260623_4712158.html). No speculative Line 22, M101, Line 13 split, Line 1 branch or Daxing Airport Express northern extension is drawn. Gaojiayuan, Hongmiao and Taoranqiao on Line 14 also remain unopened.
