### Names: decisions and remaining evidence gaps

- The 1984 northern section is labelled **Second Phase**, then **Loop Line** from 1987-12-28, then **Line 2** from 2002-07-24, following the [Chinese system chronology](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/北京地铁). The last exact day is a secondary historical reference, not a newly recovered primary naming notice. “Line 1” is used as the English name of the original first-phase service; the later Chinese change from 一线 to 1号线 does not create a different English name.
- **Fuba Line → Line 1**, 2000-06-28; **Airport Express → Capital Airport Express**, 2019-09-24 ([contemporary report](https://ie.bjd.com.cn/a/201909/24/AP5d89ca83e4b021e796143804.html)); **Line 1 / Batong**, 2021-08-29, models the merged service and permanent retirement of the redundant Sihui/Batong and Sihui Dong/Line 1 platforms. It is a combined service label, not a claim that the two infrastructure lines ceased to have administrative identities.
- **Broadcasting Institute → Communication University of China**, 2007-04-11, follows the April 12 contemporary report cited by [the station history](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/传媒大学站) ([archived report](https://web.archive.org/web/20171205143554/http://news.163.com/07/0412/18/3BT8B3GM000120GU.html)). The university’s 2004 rename was not the station rename.
- **City Railway / Line 13:** the numerical designation was already used at opening ([contemporary 2002 report](https://news.sohu.com/22/35/news203453522.shtml)); a [2025 retrospective](https://xinwen.bjd.com.cn/content/s6940aa98e4b06b6f7a7f8649.html) instead describes 2003-12-31 as formal naming. The map uses Line 13 from its first public day, without presenting the retrospective as a definite rename. **Olympic Branch / Line 8** likewise coexisted as names; it is not given a fabricated rename date.
- **Unresolved historical names:** Lixin → Gongzhufen (1980s), Bajiaocun → Bajiao Amusement Park (1990s), Xinhua Jie → Heping Men (1987), and Gucheng Lu → Gucheng (2008) lack verified exact days in the retrieved evidence. Markers retain current names; Line 1's 1971 terminus was then called Lixin. [Beijing Daily’s archive investigation](https://news.bjd.com.cn/2025/09/24/11321556.shtml) specifically contradicts treating the amusement park’s 1986 opening as the station rename. [The January 31, 2008 Gucheng reconstruction report](https://news.sina.com.cn/c/2008-01-31/021913356273s.shtml) still uses Gucheng Lu; the February 1 facility opening is not evidence of an exact rename day. Do not “complete” these by inventing January 1 dates.
- English names use consistent current translations across a physical station. Beijing’s 2020–24 English-signage revisions were gradual and differed by operator/station; they are not modelled as simultaneous station renames. Qinghe’s added Chinese 站 is not a new English station identity. The proposed 2026 Tongzhou Beiguan rename is not recorded as an implemented change.
- **Line 1 1971–1972 and the Olympic branch (restricted access):** 1971's 试运营 sold tickets
  only against work-unit letters, and unrestricted sale began 1972-12-27
  ([Beijing Subway chronicle](https://web.archive.org/web/2013/http://www.bjsubway.com/node/1842)).
  Line 8's Olympic branch carried only Olympic ticket and credential holders until 2008-10-09
  ([Qianlong via Sina](https://travel.sina.com.cn/around/2008-10-10/114429534.shtml)). Under the
  spec §7 rule restricted-access service counts, so both appear on the earlier date with events
  naming the restricted service; the later opening to all passengers (1972-12-27, 2008-10-09) and
  Line 1's formal opening (1981-09-15) are separate events. Whether organised groups of citizens rode Line 1 in
  1969–1970, before trial operation, is not established (the 1965–1970 chronicle page was not
  retrieved); the recorded 1971-01-15 stays. Line 4's 2009-08-31 ride for about 200 relocated
  residents ([北京地铁4号线](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/北京地铁4号线)) was a one-off thank-you
  event, not public riding, and is not drawn. No other line had public rides before its recorded
  opening in the sources checked (Lines 5, 13, Batong, the 2010 lines, Xijiao and Yizhuang T1).

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

- **No starting map artwork:** railway ways, stop positions, Beijing’s municipal boundary ([OSM relation 912940](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/912940)) and water geometry were retrieved on **2026-09-24** from [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/), © OpenStreetMap contributors, [ODbL 1.0](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). The SVG and preview are derived, edited geographic illustrations. The logo is [AlgaeGraphix’s public-domain geometric artwork](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beijing_Subway_simplified_logo.svg), with JaJaWa’s official-colour revision. Stations on Beijing MTR's Lines 4, 14, 16, 17, 19 and the Daxing Line also show Beijing MTR's own emblem from each line's opening, cropped from [its Chinese Wikipedia logo file](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BJMTR_logo.svg) without the “京港地铁 BJMTR” lettering. That file is marked non-free (a trademark used under fair use).
- Coordinates use **WGS84 / UTM zone 50N (EPSG:32650)**, then `x = (easting − 408000) / 20`, `y = (4466000 − northing) / 20`, in a `4400 × 5300` viewBox. This places 1 km at 50 SVG units. Track, water and land use the same projection. The [Amap current network](https://map.amap.com/service/subway?srhdata=1100_drw_beijing.json) cross-checks current stops and English spellings; Zhufang Bei’s missing OSM stop position uses Amap coordinates with **GCJ-02 converted to WGS84**, projected onto the mapped railway.
- Curves follow rail-way vertices, simplified at 9 m and interpolated with cubic Béziers. Local station-scale offsets keep interchange lines legible; they are cartographic adjustments, not engineering survey geometry. Contiguous opening spans remain single paths, split only for actual historical changes, reassignments or reroutes. No per-station track fragmentation, station text, legend artwork or background labels are embedded.
- The original Line 1 connector uses [OSM way 114647613](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/114647613). The pre-2021 parallel Sihui–Sihui Dong alignment uses mapped railway ways, with exaggerated platform separation for legibility. Qinghe’s old alignment uses **2018-01-01 OSM history**, replaced on 2019-02-17. Xi’erqi’s old marker is approximate, as noted above. Older small track shifts and rebuilt platform footprints without recovered engineering drawings remain generalized; present-day geometry is not proof that every metre was unchanged since opening.
- Capital Airport Express includes both the outbound route and the return branch from [relation 2062999](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/2062999). Its reversing Terminal 3 spur is traversed twice by the continuous SVG path, but physical route kilometres are counted once. It is not an invented triangle between airport station points.
- The geography is **present-day throughout playback**. Beijing land is the normal land colour; neighbouring Hebei is the foreign-land colour, including the Daxing Airport approach. Lakes and mapped riverbank polygons preserve holes; river/canal centreline buffers fill gaps where OSM has no bank polygon. Those small-watercourse widths are cartographic estimates, not historical or surveyed banks. Land and water simplification tolerances are 12 m and 7 m respectively.
- Xizhimen, Dongzhimen, Sihui and Sihui Dong retain their separate-fare/out-of-station phases. Muxidi and Dazhongsi have distinct station IDs; circle-to-capsule replacements share an identity with dated `--YYYY-MM-DD` versions. Pingguoyuan’s former Line 1 station and newer 6/S1 complex are separate until the 2026 internal connection. Xijiao/T1 have tracks only except memberships at Bagou/Rongchang Dongjie, following the simplified-service rule.
- **Kilometres are approximate by opening stage.** Modern totals use the published line overviews, checked against [the operator’s interstation-distance tables](https://www.mtr.bj.cn/service/line/distable/line-1.html). These definitions differ: construction length, running length and station-centre distance can include different turnbacks/overruns. Values are allocated and rounded to one decimal per historical span; they are not SVG arc lengths. The sum currently shown is **899.6 km**, not the municipal **909 km** headline. That definition/allocation discrepancy remains unresolved; the map does not force an arbitrary extra 9.4 km into a section. Tram stops are deliberately excluded from the station statistic, and Line 1/Batong is one current legend entry, so app counts must not be equated with the official “30 lines / 541 stations” per-line inventory.

<a id="nanjing"></a>

## Nanjing (`nanjing`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/nanjing/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/nanjing/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/nanjing/map.svg).

Checked through **2026-09-24**. The map includes the fifteen operating metro/suburban lines
(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, S1, S2, S3, S4, S6, S7, S8, S9), plus Hexi and Qilin trams as
simplified tracks. S4 and the trams are the operator's own lines (spec §8). S4 includes its operating Chuzhou section; the unbuilt connection into
Nanjing and its reserved stations are not shown. Lines 6, 9, 11 and the other announced
extensions are not treated as open. The [September 23 operator service announcement](https://www.nanjing.gov.cn/zzb/hdhy/hygq_72666/202609/t20260923_5916215.html)
and [April S2 opening report](https://www.jiangning.gov.cn/sjb/xwzx/gzdt/202604/t20260424_5829714.html)
were checked alongside the individual line histories. This is a construction history:
COVID, flooding, repairs, service hours and temporary testing suspensions do not remove
unchanged infrastructure.

### Opening and conversion chronology

The English and Chinese [system history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Metro),
[station inventory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nanjing_Metro_stations) and individual
line articles were used as indexes, then compared with contemporary reports. In particular,
under the spec §7 rule Line 1 appears on May 15, 2005 with weekend sightseeing (观光运营)
between Xinjiekou and Xiaohang. The weekend sightseeing ended on July 31 and the line carried
no public until August 12 (a pause the map does not draw, spec §7), when every station between Maigaoqiao and Xiaohang opened with daily
fare-paying "simulated operation" (模拟运营), which reached Olympic Stadium on August 26. The
September 3 start of trial operation (试运营), the regular opening, is its own event.

The "Map change" column summarises each date's `events.json` descriptions rather than copying them.

### Geometry, identities and distance

- Drawn from railway ways and stop positions in [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/),
  © OpenStreetMap contributors, [ODbL 1.0](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), retrieved
  September 24, 2026. All railways and geography share EPSG:32650, at 50 SVG units/km.
- Current route relations: 1533791, 3413088, 7885542, 9588280, 17417176, 15336345,
  1529760, 7913265, 19979191, 7913253, 15804056, 13200480, 9584584, 9588173,
  9584574; tram routes 16159337 and 16159339. These supply alignment, not opening dates.
- The retired Andemen approach is recovered from pre-conversion relation 1529760/version 19;
  the old Hexi southern alignment from way 736715174/version 9. Recovering deleted OSM
  nodes is a cartographic reconstruction, not evidence of service dates. The reusable track
  north/west of those changes is not duplicated into one path per station interval.
- Background land is present-day Jiangsu, relation 913012; Anhui has the foreign-land fill.
  Yangtze bank polygons preserve islands; Xuanwu, Mochou, Shijiu, Gucheng and Jinniu lakes
  use mapped polygons. Historical shoreline changes are not animated. Minor ponds and streams
  are omitted. Curves simplify mapped vertices, and local station offsets keep capsules straight
  and nearby non-serving lines clear; they are not survey drawings.
- Marker versions share a stable identity through circle-to-capsule upgrades. Zhushanlu is the
  explicit out-of-station exception. Tram stops are omitted apart from their existing heavy-rail
  interchange markers, per the shared specification.
- The current inventory has **293 line/platform memberships at 260 distinct marker identities**.
  Official headline station totals often count a transfer once for each line: the December 2025
  announcement's 267 equals the sum of platform counts before adding S2's sixteen and S4's ten.
- `data-km` uses published route/section lengths rounded to tenths; the early Line 1 sightseeing
  and reused western sections are apportioned within the published line totals. These subdivisions
  are approximate, not surveyed distances. Current metro/suburban paths sum to **624.5 km**;
  including the simplified trams gives **641.3 km**. This does not exactly reproduce the roughly
  625.7 km headline metro total: published construction and operating lengths differ. No invisible
  length or phantom track was added to force a match.
- [Nanjing Metro logo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nanjing_Metro_Logo.svg): public-domain
  geometric mark; the Commons SVG was corrected by Tomchen1989 using the operator's mark.

### Remaining evidence gaps

These are limitations, not verified exact-date claims:

1. **Early sightseeing extensions:** contemporary reports establish the May 15 Xinjiekou–Xiaohang
   sightseeing and the August 12 all-station service. Earlier plans mentioned June trips to Gulou
   and July trips to Maigaoqiao, but no implemented start date was established for either (a later
   personal account describes a June 4 Gulou trip). The map does not invent June 1 / July 1 dates,
   so track north of Xinjiekou starts on August 12. The May 12 rehearsal for invited press and
   newspaper readers is not drawn: how the readers were chosen is unknown, so it is not shown to
   have been open to the public (spec §7).
2. **Linjiang / YOGSP:** a secondary station account places the addition of “YOGSP” in December
   2016, without a verified day. The stable base name **Linjiang** is retained across the timeline;
   the full later suffix and its transition remain unencoded. It is not backdated to opening.
3. **Caochangmen and Xuzhuang subtitles:** Chinese institutional prefixes changed to subtitles in 2018. The cited approval is February 13; reports describe implementation in March. The map uses
   the English base names throughout, rather than claiming a synchronized English signage change
   on the approval date. Other inconsistent English abbreviations in the network (CPU, NJCI,
   NMU / JIETT) likewise do not establish dated operational renames.
4. **Invited-group rides not counted:** Line 2's 23–26 May 2010 "部分市民代表试乘" (citizen
   representatives, known only from Baidu Baike) is not treated as public riding; Line 2 keeps
   its recorded opening.

Validation checks SVG/legend/event boundary agreement, station memberships, unique IDs, path counts
and distances. Browser checks exercise all event dates and adjacent days in both directions,
search identities, highlighted-line filtering, tooltip dismissal, mobile resize and the home preview.
These checks validate the implementation; they do not resolve the historical evidence gaps above.

<a id="chongqing"></a>

## Chongqing — Rail Transit (`chongqing`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/chongqing/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/chongqing/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/chongqing/map.svg).
Research cutoff: **24 September 2026**. New geographic artwork, not a converted network diagram.

### Scope and line histories

Includes Lines 1, 2, 3 (including its airport branch), 4, 5, 6 (including the Chongqing East branch),
9, 10, 18, the Loop Line, International Expo Line, Jiangtiao, Bitong and the simplified Bishan
SkyShuttle. The Expo branch has its own legend identity, using its longstanding 国博线 name.
The 3 and 6 branches retain their parent line identity. Through trains on 4/Loop/5 and 5/Jiangtiao
do not duplicate the underlying infrastructure.

Openings follow the spec §7 opening rule: the first day the public could ride, including paid
sightseeing, trial operation, free trial rides and experience weeks. Temporary maintenance, accident, epidemic and integration-test
suspensions do not erase built lines. No never-opened stations or proposed extensions are drawn.
This is the rail-transit network, not every historical transport mode in Chongqing: the separate
river cableways, funiculars, escalators, national railways and scenic park rides are outside scope.

The following secondary line histories and their station tables were read as an inventory and
cross-checked with dated announcements. They also index intermediate stations not named in the
short event descriptions. Recovered Weibo/WeChat citations are identified explicitly; recovering
a citation does not mean the original post was independently retrievable.

### Date and interchange decisions

- **Line 2:** the first public rides were paid sightseeing, followed by trial running and then
  regular service; every stage is drawn (spec §7). Contemporary Chongqing papers carried on Sina
  (event rows above) establish which stations passengers could board or leave at:
  - **2004-11-06, Daping–Zoo, weekend mornings.** Tickets were sold only at Daping and Zoo. Trains
    paused at Yuanjiagang, Xiejiawan and Yangjiaping so riders could look at the platforms, then went
    on. Nobody could start or end a journey there, so only the termini are shown.
  - **2004-12-11, Jiaochangkou–Zoo, weekends.** Riders could board or alight only at Jiaochangkou,
    Daxigou, Daping and Zoo ("只在大溪沟和大坪停留上下客").
  - **2004-12-28, daily trial running.** Nine stations: Jiaochangkou, Linjiangmen, Daxigou,
    Niujiaotuo, Liziba, Daping, Yuanjiagang, Yangjiaping and Zoo. Huanghuayuan, Zengjiayan,
    Fotuguan and Xiejiawan were skipped.
  - **Later stations.** Huanghuayuan opened 2005-02-09, Xiejiawan by 2005-03-31 (display bound, day
    unreported), Fotuguan 2005-04-09 and Zengjiayan 2005-06-15 (zh-wiki; bounded by contemporary
    reports). Regular service (正式运行) began 2005-06-18
    ([People's Daily Chongqing, 2020](http://cq.people.com.cn/n2/2020/0618/c365405-34095403.html)).
  - **Not counted.** The October 2004 载人模拟运行 carried invited riders only. zh-wiki's
    2005-06-18 (Huanghuayuan) and 2006-07-10 (Xiejiawan) conflict with the contemporary reports and
    are not used. The 2004 sightseeing and trial-running fares are not recorded (spec §10).
- **Gaomiaocun:** October 17, 2011, as in the Chinese station chronology and contemporary
  October 13 announcement. The English opening table's November 17 date is inconsistent.
- **Line 6 north:** December 31, 2013 adds five operating stations, including Jinshansi.
  Caojiawan, Xiangjiagang and Tiansheng open later. An opening table that counts four omitted Jinshansi.
- **Bitong:** appears on December 26, 2024 with the free "欢乐体验周" (happy experience week),
  which ran without a break to the January 2, 2025 start of 初期运营, recorded as the opening
  (spec §7). Bishan is an
  out-of-station interchange during the week, because riders changing to Line 1 had to leave the
  gates, and in-station from January 2 ([12371.gov.cn](https://m.12371.gov.cn/content/2024-12/24/content_480523.html);
  [CNR](https://cq.cnr.cn/jr/20250107/t20250107_527033802.shtml) "支持站内换乘"). Qinglonghu was not
  one of the eight opened stations.
- **SkyShuttle:** free public trial rides at five stations, including both termini, ran February
  15–24, 2021 ([Chongqing Daily via chinanews](http://www.cq.chinanews.com.cn/wap/news/2021/0222/39-19761.html)).
  The line then carried no public until regular operation on April 16; that pause is not drawn
  (spec §7), so the SkyShuttle stays on the map from February 15.
  Individual SkyShuttle stops are omitted under the shared simplified-service rule.
- **Paid areas:** Shapingba's Line 1, Loop and Line 9 markers remain separate until September 30,
  2022; Xiejiawan's Line 2/Loop markers merge June 17, 2023. Guanyinqiao, Xietaizi, Yangjiaping and
  Yudaishan remain outside interchanges. Xietaizi has three separate station identities after its
  delayed Line 18 opening. The Line 18 opening notice identifies Fuhualu, Olympic Sports Center,
  Baijusi and Tiaodeng as in-station transfers from opening; no invented later conversion is added.
  See the [2026 operator network map](https://jtj.cq.gov.cn/zwgk_240/zfxxgkml/gggs/tzgg/202603/W020260302622398077574.pdf)
  and the dated passage notices above. The PDF's indexed text was available; direct PDF download
  was unavailable during this audit.
- **Cutoff:** Shunshuisi Park, Xinqiao, Youdiangang, Nanping's Line 10 platform and Qinglonghu
  remain absent. Line 15 is not opened merely because its fare was published:
  [September 8 fare notice](https://fzggw.cq.gov.cn/zwgk/zfxxgkml/jgxx/jgzc/202609/t20260908_16048650.html),
  [August pre-opening safety assessment](https://jtysw.cq.gov.cn/sy_240/bmdt/202608/t20260819_15951204.html),
  [September 19 power-up report](https://www.cqnews.net/web/content_1550770814051643392.html).
  Future project completion targets are not passenger opening dates.

### Rename rollout qualifications

These are implementation-date choices supported by dated reports, not claims that every sign
changed simultaneously:

1. **Chongqing North → Chongqing North Station South Square:** April 7, 2016 starts the reported
   formal rollout. Some signs were visible on March 22; the project was scheduled to finish April 30.
   [March signage report](https://news.ifeng.com/a/20160323/48123672_0.shtml), April report above.
2. **Jiangbei Airport → Terminal 2 of Jiangbei Airport:** December 25, 2017 is the dated new map
   attestation. Secondary accounts also give December 26 or the December 28 Line 10 opening;
   the exact first day of every English sign/announcement was not established.
3. **Pingchang → Happy Valley:** January 12, 2018 is the formal rename reported on January 19.
   [New platform signs were already reported December 3, 2017](https://www.cqtitle.com/new/gd/2017/1204/16876.html),
   while other signs and announcements still used Pingchang. Proposal/approval dates in March/July
   2017 are not treated as completed passenger-name changes.
4. **Four university names:** the operator starts the batch on December 1, 2019; physical signage
   work continues into March 2020. See the [university's rollout explanation](https://dwxcbwlgzb.swu.edu.cn/info/1028/3316.htm).
   Construction names and unimplemented proposals do not create passenger-history states.

### Geography, identity and distance

- Route alignments, stop locations, riverbanks and administrative boundaries are derived from
  [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/), © OpenStreetMap contributors,
  [ODbL 1.0](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), retrieved September 24, 2026.
  All layers use EPSG:32648, at 18 metres per SVG unit. River polygons preserve islands and the
  Yangtze/Jialing confluence; Sichuan beyond the Chongqing boundary uses the foreign-land fill.
  Shorelines represent the current geography, not an animated hydrological history.
- OSM route relations: 2336457, 2353578, 2341149, 9597503, 7677819, 7913722, 2768661,
  19293566, 3474487, 14004563, 8300862, 15749313, 7662492, 10176833, 17135615 and 12759727.
  Chongqing boundary: 913069. These establish geometry, not historical service dates.
- Smooth cubic curves follow mapped railway ways, with local station offsets for readable straight
  interchange capsules and clearance from lines that do not serve a station. Shapingba's platforms
  are placed along their existing tracks on a common capsule axis, avoiding artificial sharp bends.
  The drawing is geographically based, not a survey or a claim of exact platform dimensions.
- There are 44 track paths, split at historical openings rather than every station, and 325 dated
  marker versions. At the cutoff, 276 marker identities are present. Separate outside interchanges
  count separately; simplified SkyShuttle stops do not inflate the heavy-rail station count.
- Published kilometres come from opening reports and the operator group's
  [April 2026 bond prospectus, printed pages 25–26](https://static.sse.com.cn/disclosure/bond/announcement/company/c/new/2026-04-22/245126_20260422_2LAT.pdf).
  Its opening-date column contains transcription errors and is not used to override contemporary
  opening notices. Lengths are rounded to tenths. Early staged Line 1/2/3 sections are apportioned
  within published totals; those subdivisions are estimates. Line 4's west section is approximately
  9.5 km after excluding the unopened 1.267 km Shunshuisi Park interval from the 10.8 km project;
  Line 9 excludes the unopened Xinqiao tail. Construction/project lengths therefore need not equal
  the sum of drawn passenger sections. No hidden track or length is added to force a headline total. Current drawn sections sum to 575.5 km, or 590.9 km including SkyShuttle.
- [CRT logo source](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chongqing_Rail_Transit_logo.svg): the existing
  green emblem is retained in its original proportions, with the accompanying wordmark omitted.
  The mark identifies the network; it is not newly drawn or an endorsement.

Validation: the spec checker, every event and adjacent day in forward/reverse playback, station
search (including historical names and separate same-name stations), line-filtered search,
tooltip dismissal, mobile resize, home preview and actual Bézier-to-marker clearance.
The checks validate the implementation, not the unresolved exact-day rollout questions above.

<a id="xian"></a>

## Xi'an (`xian`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/xian/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/xian/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/xian/map.svg).
New map and research, **27 September 2026**. New geographic artwork drawn from OpenStreetMap, not a converted network diagram.

### Scope

The map follows the operator's current official network map ([西安轨道交通线网示意图 / Xi'an Metro System Map][xa-official-map], version of 2026-06-29): Lines 1–6, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16 and the **Xihu Line**, which the map draws as a normal legend line with its two open stations. The Xihu Line runs over national-rail track, but Xi'an Metro sells its tickets and runs its passenger service (China Railway Xi'an Group dispatches the trains), so it passes both scope tests (spec §8). Xianyang sections of Xi'an Metro lines (Line 1 phases 2 and 3, Lines 5, 14 and 16) are included.

- **Line 14 and the Airport Intercity.** The 西安北至机场城际 (Airport Intercity) opened on 2019-09-29 under 陕西城际铁路有限公司, a Shaanxi Railway Group company, with separate fares. Xi'an Metro took over its management from 2021-01-01 and merged it into Line 14 on 2021-06-29. Whether Xi'an Metro's 2019–20 maps drew it is not established; it is included as Line 14's predecessor (spec §8's operator family includes predecessors), labelled **Airport Intercity** until the merger, with a dated operator handover.
- **Excluded:** the Hi-Tech Zone SkyShuttle (西安云巴, also called the Hi-Tech Zone tram test line; opened 2024-08-12, run by 西安云巴交通运营有限公司 for the district, own fares, not on the official map); the out-of-service Qujiang sightseeing monorail and Kunming Lake ART line (tourist operators); national rail; Line 17 and other lines under construction; the Xihu Line's three unopened stations (昆明池, 马王, 五竹).
- **Own-land shading:** Xi'an's municipal boundary ([OSM relation 3226004][xa-osm-boundary]) is the own land. Xianyang (including the Xianyang parts of Xixian New Area and the airport), Weinan and the other neighbours use the outside-land colour; Line 1's phase 2 and 3 sections, the western parts of Lines 5 and 16 and most of Line 14 run across it.

Openings follow spec §7. Three lines had free public trial rides before opening and appear with those rides and stay on the map through the opening (spec §7), which is its own "opens" event: Line 2 (2011-09-08 – 11; tickets handed out through line-side communities), Line 1 (2013-09-09 – 10; trial-ride tickets) and the Airport Intercity (2019-09-23 – 24; free vouchers at any station, no ID needed). Every other pre-opening ride found (media, invited residents, 试乘证 holders, "体验官", open days) was invitation-only and is not drawn: Line 3 (2016-09-01), Line 4 (2018-12), Line 1 phase 2 (2019-09-22), Lines 5/6/9 (2020-12-07 – 09), Line 14 (2021-03-21, 2021-06-25), Xihu (2022-10-01), Line 6 phase 2 (2022-12-25), Line 1 phase 3 (2023-09-16), 2024-09-19 – 22, Line 8 (2024-12-22), Line 15 (2025-12-23) and 西安东站 (2026-06-26). No pre-opening rides were found for Line 2's 2014 and 2023 extensions, Line 16 or 机场（T5）; searches are not proof of absence. Temporary suspensions (including the December 2021 – January 2022 lockdown) are not drawn.

### Primary records and focused references

- [Official network map, 2026-06-29][xa-official-map] — **New**. Scope, legend colours, interchange symbols and the current English (romanised) station names; transcribed for all 248 stations. The operator's station API (`api-basicdata/lineStation/findLineAll`) was also read but is stale for renamed and new stations.
- [华商报 via Sina, 2011-03-25][xa-pinyin-2011] — **New**. "西安地铁一、二号线英文站名全部采用大写汉语拼音译法…北客站翻译成BEIKEZHAN". Xi'an has used capitalised Hanyu Pinyin station names since opening; every later renaming notice gives the "罗马字母拼写".
- [Xi'an Civil Affairs Bureau, 2022-09-20 (archived)][xa-rename-2022], [西部网, 2023-06-26][xa-rename-2023] and [Sina, 2025-07-25][xa-rename-2025] — **New**. Dated renames.
- [Operator colour reply on 人民网, 2020-04-08 (archived)][xa-colours-2020] — **New**. Pantone references for Lines 1–4 (3005 C, Red 032 C, 252 U, 319 C); Lines 5, 6 and 9 are 374 U, 2726 C and 1375 C in other replies.
- Each event row below cites the notices and reports behind that date.

**English names.** Labels use the official romanisation exactly as spelled and spaced on the 2026 map and in the renaming notices, written with ordinary pinyin capitalisation (GB/T 16159) instead of the all-capitals signage typography: `ZHONGLOU` → `Zhonglou`, `FENGCHENG 10 LU` → `Fengcheng 10 Lu`, `XI'AN BEIZHAN` → `Xi'an Beizhan`, `SHIDI-SANYIYUAN` → `Shidi-Sanyiyuan`. The airport stations keep their English (`Airport W.(T1/T2/T3)`, `Airport(T5)`); the commas of `AIRPORT W.(T1,T2,T3)` become slashes, as in the operator's API, because label syntax forbids commas (spec §2). Line 4's 北客站（北广场） is `Beikezhan (Beiguangchang)` from its signage (zh.wikipedia and Commons photographs). Lines are named `Line N`, `Xihu Line` and `Airport Intercity`.

**Logos and licences.**

- `xian-metro.svg`: the Xi'an Metro city-wall emblem, from [en.wikipedia File:Xian_Metro_logo.svg][xa-logo] (a local non-free file tagged SVG-Logo and Trademark, author given as Xi'an Metro Group). Graphic only, no lettering; its paths and colour are unchanged, with a comment added.
- `xazt.svg`: 西安中铁轨道交通有限公司 (XAZT), the China Railway (60 %) / Xi'an Rail Transit Group (40 %) PPP company that has run Line 9 under a 30-year BOT concession since it opened ([company profile][xa-xazt]). No vector or Commons file exists; the emblem was redrawn as vector geometry from the company's raster footer logo, with the "XAZT" lettering removed from its band. All rights reserved by the company; used for identification only.
- `shaanxi-railway.svg`: the emblem of 陕西省铁路集团 (Shaanxi Province Railway Group), parent of 陕西城际铁路有限公司, redrawn as vector from the group's raster logo on its archived site without the lettering. No logo of the subsidiary itself was found. All rights reserved; used for identification only.
- Both redrawn marks were rendered and compared with their sources (about 0.87–0.88 overlap ratio, the difference being the removed lettering and anti-aliasing).

### Interchanges, identities and names

- **In-station from opening:** every interchange except the two below; the zh.wikipedia station articles and opening notices describe station-hall, vertical, cross-platform or passage transfers inside the paid area (北大街 "不用出站", 2013; 行政中心 "台台换乘", 2018; 西安工大·武德路, 井上村 and the Line 8 and 15 interchanges in their opening notices).
- **西安北站 (Lines 2, 4, 14):** separate stations until 2021-06-29 (Line 2 circle; Line 4 circle, joined by the Airport Intercity's cross-platform capsule from 2019-09-29), with a connector; one capsule from the 287 m paid-area corridor. The capsule continues the Line 2 station's identity (the earliest) and name until both were renamed 西安北站 on 2022-09-20.
- **阿房宫南 (Line 5 / Xihu):** connector from 2022-11-01, capsule from 2023-09-26.
- **双寨 (Lines 3 / 14), 2021-06-29:** drawn in-station. The operator designates it an interchange; the zh.wikipedia station article describes a transfer building between the elevated Line 3 and underground Line 14 stations and a separate unpaid link ("非付费区设独立连通道"). **UNVERIFIED:** no official statement that the transfer stays inside the paid area was found (one guide says "出站后").
- **Not interchanges:** 木塔寺 (Line 6) and 木塔寺西 (Line 8) ("8号线与6号线暂时无法在此换乘"); the Line 8 marker is moved along its track so the two circles stay 21 units apart. 祝村, 丈八四路 and 鱼化寨 connect to the excluded SkyShuttle only.
- **Renames recorded:** 北客站 / 北客站（北广场） → 西安北站 (2022-09-20); 会展中心 → 电视塔 and 运动公园 → 凤城十路 (2023-06-27, announced 2023-06-26); 纬一街 → 八里村, 市图书馆 → 青少年中心, 元朔路 → 元鼎路 (2025-12-22, display bound). 火车站 → 西安站 happened before that station opened, and 李家村 / 鲁家村 / 雁南四路 were renamed before Line 4 opened, so neither is a map change.
- **Not modelled:** the numbered-road format change (`FENGCHENG 5-LU` → `FENGCHENG 5 LU`, `WEI 1-JIE` → `WEI 1 JIE`), which zh.wikipedia places around June 2023 without a primary source; current forms are used throughout. Line 3's secondary names 延兴门（沙坡） and 香湖湾（黄邓） are not on the official map or in the operator API. The English names used on the Airport Intercity in 2019–21 were not found; current forms are used.

### SVG geography, identities and measurement limits

- **No starting artwork:** route relations (Lines 1–6, 8–10, 14–16 and Xihu; e.g. [OSM 7869252][xa-osm-1], [OSM 18462995][xa-osm-8], [OSM 10381396][xa-osm-14], [OSM 16494759][xa-osm-xihu]) were retrieved on **2026-09-27** from the OpenStreetMap API; water and the municipal boundary come from [Geofabrik's Shaanxi extract][xa-geofabrik] of **2026-09-23**. © OpenStreetMap contributors, [ODbL 1.0](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).
- **Projection:** WGS84 / UTM zone 49N (EPSG:32649), `x = (easting − 275000) / 20`, `y = (3827000 − northing) / 20`: 20 m per SVG unit, as Beijing and Nanjing. `initialBounds` is `3400 × 2800` (the network plus about 5 km); the canvas is `-1965 -416 7300 4500`, the smallest found whose minimum-zoom view and all four constrained pan corners keep the latest network at least 13 px inside the clear area (24 px from the Stats, Changelog and legend panels) at 1280 × 720, 1280 × 800, 1366 × 768, 1440 × 900 and 1536 × 864.
- **Tracks:** railway ways chained per route, stations projected onto them; smooth cubic Béziers through the mapped vertices, with local PCHIP offsets so that platforms of one interchange share a straight capsule axis (spacing one marker width, 17 units for out-of-station pairs). Tracks split only at historical openings (23 paths); Line 8 is one closed loop from 东等驾坡.
- **Water and land:** principal river corridors (Wei, Jing, Ba, Chan, Feng, Jue, Lao, Hei, Zao, Qing, Shichuan) with mapped banks and a thin centreline symbol where banks are missing; lakes and reservoirs at least 150 overview pixels²; the Ming city-wall moat, Xingqing, Qujiang, Hancheng, Yanming and Kunming Lake kept as landmarks. Selection at the whole-network overview, simplification 0.35 units. Rivers end where OSM stops tagging them `waterway=river`. The background is present-day geography throughout playback.
- **Kilometres:** published section lengths where given (above); the Line 2 phase 1 split, the Line 5 east split and the rounding of Line 14 (13.65 → 13.7) are allocations. Current drawn sections sum to 448.1 km, 421.8 km without the Xihu Line.
- **Operators:** `metro` (Xi'an Metro) by default; Line 9's markers show `xazt`; Airport Intercity markers show `intercity` until 2021-01-01, then `metro`. Lines 5, 6, 14 and 16 are operated by Xi'an Metro's operating branch (Line 16 was built by a Xixian New Area company).

Validation: the spec checker, the repository tests, marker-to-line clearance on every change date, renders of each preview and interchange change, and the app in a headless browser (no console errors; scrubbing to 2011-09-08, 2019-09-24 and today; station tooltips).

<a id="seoul"></a>

## Seoul (`seoul`)

Assets: [events](../src/assets/seoul/data/events.json), [line names](../src/assets/seoul/data/lines.json), [SVG](../src/assets/seoul/map.svg).

Added **25 September 2026**. `/seoul` covers metropolitan electric passenger service from
**1974-08-15**: Seoul Lines 1–9, both Incheon lines, Korail's metropolitan branches, AREX,
Shinbundang, Seohae, Incheon Airport Maglev, the five light-rail systems and the two open GTX-A
sections, as drawn on the official Seoul Metropolitan Subway map (spec §8). The Incheon Airport
Maglev is historical only (2016-02-03 to 2022-07-14). Conventional railway service before electrification, intercity KTX/SRT/ITX services,
freight, depot tracks without passenger service, Wolmi Sea Train and unbuilt projects are outside
this map. The U Line's public depot-platform shuttle is included from 2021-10-30.

### Opening dates and names

- [Seoul Metro opening history](https://data.seoul.go.kr/dataList/OA-13317/S/1/datasetView.do),
  downloadable `서울교통공사_개통 현황_20250813.zip`, is the primary section-opening table for
  Lines 1–8 and the eastern Line 9 extensions. In particular, Line 7's central section opened
  **2000-08-01**, and Line 4 opened in two stages in 1985; the whole original line did not open
  on its first day.
- [Seoul Historiography Institute's subway history](https://history.seoul.go.kr/ebook/getFile/prACysRcyFR/pdf)
  and [Gyeonggi's city-construction history](https://memory.library.kr/files/original/34bdfb747e6b17d752c7996a246e7b7a.pdf)
  corroborate early construction. The latter dates Seongbuk–Chang-dong to **1985-04-20**;
  Wolgye and Nokcheon followed on **1985-08-22**. Some station articles incorrectly assign
  the later date to the entire extension.
- The [Line 1 chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_Subway_Line_1),
  [Gyeongui–Jungang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongui%E2%80%93Jungang_Line),
  [Suin–Bundang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suin%E2%80%93Bundang_Line),
  [Gyeongchun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongchun_Line),
  [Gyeonggang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeonggang_Line),
  [AREX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AREX),
  [Shinbundang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinbundang_Line),
  [Seohae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seohae_Line),
  [Incheon 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Subway_Line_1), and
  [Incheon 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon_Subway_Line_2) histories supply the
  metropolitan extensions. The individual English and Korean station histories supply infill
  dates, renames and transfer changes. Line 1's English chronology contains incorrect dates for
  Garibong → Gasan Digital Complex and Bugok → Uiwang; the Korean station histories date these
  **2005-07-01** and **2004-06-25**, respectively.
- Light-rail references: [Ui–Sinseol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ui_LRT),
  [Sillim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sillim_Line),
  [Gimpo Goldline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimpo_Goldline),
  [EverLine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EverLine), and
  [U Line operator's station list](https://www.ulrt.co.kr/doc/contents/information/stations.php).
  Per the shared map convention, these five systems have thin tracks and memberships at their
  heavy-rail interchanges, without individual light-rail stop markers. Incheon Line 2 is shown
  with all stations, as a primary Incheon subway line.
- Recent openings: [Incheon government's Geomdan notice](https://www.incheon.go.kr/mayor_8/MA040101/view?repSeq=DOM_0000000012563847)
  confirms **2025-06-28**; [MOLIT's GTX-A notice](https://www.molit.go.kr/USR/NEWS/dtl.jsp?id=95090716)
  distinguishes the northern and southern services. GTX-A's unconnected middle section is not
  drawn as open. [Seoul's Dongbuk construction record](https://cis.seoul.go.kr/TotalAlimi_new/PopInfo.action?cmd=info1&pjt_cd=1112018081799)
  and [Wirye testing notice](https://www.seoul.go.kr/news/news_report.do?nttNo=450817)
  describe construction/testing, not passenger openings; neither is included.
- Wikipedia's March 2026 forecast for the Wonsi–Seohwaseong connection is stale:
  [Chosun's March 11 report](https://realty.chosun.com/site/data/html_dir/2026/03/11/2026031103418.html)
  confirms the opening was delayed, with no replacement date established. It is not shown as open.
- Temporary Dorasan restrictions and repair shutdowns do not erase built infrastructure.
- **Pre-opening public rides (spec §7):** the U Line appears on **2012-06-29**, when free public
  test rides began after the opening ceremony ([Seoul Shinmun, 30 June 2012](https://www.seoul.co.kr/news/society/2012/06/30/20120630800057)
  "29일부터 무료 시승 행사를 열고 있으며 7월1일 오전 5시 정식 개통된다"); they ran until
  regular service on 1 July, which is its own event. Not drawn: GTX-A's "국민참여 안전점검" (about 300 openly recruited
  citizens riding as a safety inspection on three unspecified days of 19–22 March 2024,
  [Aju News](https://www.ajunews.com/view/20240317095701532)) and the Sillim Line's citizen
  monitoring panel (January–February 2022, [OhmyNews](https://www.ohmynews.com/NWS_Web/View/at_pg.aspx?CNTN_CD=A0002812925)),
  which were inspections by small recruited panels rather than rides open to the public; and
  Shinbundang free rides reported for 5–12 October 2011 by a fan wiki only, with no press or
  operator confirmation (accuracy gap). The Incheon Airport Maglev, EverLine, Line 9, Ui and
  Gimpo lines had no public riding before their recorded dates.
- **Incheon Airport Maglev ends on 2022-07-14** (spec §8, lines that have left the network). It was
  suspended from that day, officially for vehicle overhaul ([ko-wiki](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/인천공항_자기부상철도);
  [Kyunghyang](https://www.khan.co.kr/article/202510191006001), which also reports about ₩8 billion
  in annual losses), and never resumed as transit: it was reclassified from urban railway to a track
  transport facility (궤도운송시설) on 2025-07-07 and left the Seoul Metropolitan Subway, then
  [reopened on 2025-10-17](https://www.incheon.go.kr/IC010205/view?repSeq=DOM_0000000013303245)
  as a free tourist ride outside the fare system. Terminal 1 returns to an AREX-only marker.
- **Line 7 operator handover on 2022-01-01:** Incheon Transit Corporation took over station,
  technical and crew operations on Kkachiul – Bupyeong-gu Office from Seoul Metro
  ([Railway Economy Daily](https://www.redaily.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=2631)); it is now
  a changelog event (spec §5).

### September 2026 verification

- **2026-07-01:** Seo-gu Office → Seohae-gu Office, Incheon Line 2. The
  [operator's station record](https://www.ictr.or.kr/main/subway/subwayStation.do?line_no=2&station_no=210)
  confirms the Korean and English names; [Doppelsoft's dated update notice](https://blog.doppelsoft.net/서해구청역-역명변경-안내7-1)
  supplies the effective date. Both names remain searchable in their historical intervals.
- No additional passenger-section opening was confirmed through **2026-09-25**. In particular,
  [Seoul's June GTX-A notice](https://www.seoul.go.kr/news/news_report.do?nttNo=459580)
  describes a potential delay beyond November, not an opening. [Wirye's city update](https://tv.seoul.go.kr/v/669e5d2c5ef540f6a3cb5f2ab7928e88)
  targets December 2026; [Gangbuk's July Dongbuk notice](https://child.gangbuk.go.kr/portal/bbs/B0000142/view.do?menuNo=200625&nttId=183175)
  targets November 2027. These remain excluded until passenger opening is confirmed.
- The Danggogae → Buramsan rename takes effect **2024-10-31** under Seoul Notice 2024-521,
  reproduced in the [operator's sign-replacement specification](https://www.g2b.go.kr/fs/fsc/fsca/fileUpload.do?k00=a2MMYzianzwExorC2swMQwxC2swNQwwC2syNgwvZGF0YS9BdHRhY2hmaWxlcy9wbnBlLzIwMjUvMDQvMTUvNzQzZjlkN2UwMDZmNDAzMGIwYjFkMmQ2OTAwYmYyNTAucGRmC2szMQwxLuqzvOyXheyngOyLnOyEnCjqs7XthrUpLnBkZgtrMjEMNWVhYzA2ZTktZTk2OC00N2M3LTk3MDYtN2I1ZmM3MTA4NzgwLDE%3D).
  October 10 was the [announcement of the naming committee's decision](https://www.yna.co.kr/amp/view/AKR20241010109500004),
  which explicitly said the formal gazette notice was still forthcoming.

The map includes **24 current lines**; Incheon Airport Maglev is historical (2016–2022). Former Bundang, Suin and
Jungang identities remain only for their historical periods; they do not add to today's line count.
Projected opening dates are not treated as completed openings.

### Historical representation

The Yongsan branch begins under Line 1, becomes the Yongsan–Deokso Line in 2005, the Jungang Line
in 2007 and joins the Gyeongui Line in 2014. Bundang and Suin retain their separate identities
until their 2020 connection. The Gwacheon/Ansan branch starts under Line 1 before joining Line 4;
residual Line 1 Ansan trains remain represented until 2003-04-30.
[Ansan City's line history](https://www.ansan.go.kr/ansanline/introduction/what-is-ansan-line)
corroborates the 1988 opening and 1994 through-running change.

Delayed stations include Geumjeong, Sanbon, Gojan, Choji, Bokjeong, Imae, Guryong, Jukjeon,
Gangmae, Hyochang Park, the four initially unopened Line 6 stations, Magok, Gangil, Cheonmasan,
Sinnae, Guseong and Seongnam. Track appears on its own opening date, without prematurely showing
these stations. Bojeong's 2004–11 surface terminal has a dated former branch and marker; the
underground replacement appears on 2011-12-28.

Transfer passages are dated at Seoul Station (2015-03-28), Cheongnyangni (2010-08-20), and
[Noryangjin (2015-10-31)](https://www.kr.or.kr/boardCnts/view.do?boardID=52&boardSeq=1103393).
Gyeongui's separate Seoul Station platforms retain a walking connector. Sinchon and Yangpyeong
homonyms are separate places. Internal supplementary-fare gates on AREX, Shinbundang and GTX
are treated as cross-operator connections within one station complex, following §6 of the spec.

### Geometry, distances and limits

Railway paths, coastlines, river polygons and the Seoul administrative boundary come from
[OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), using the
[South Korea](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/south-korea.html) and
[North Korea](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/north-korea.html) Geofabrik extracts downloaded
2026-09-25. All geometry uses UTM zone 52N at 100 SVG units/km. Missing route-relation pieces
(Jinjeop, Sinnae, Jipyeong and the public U Line depot shuttle) were recovered from connected
mapped railway ways. Station positions are aligned with those tracks. Shared corridors are
separated slightly to expose both colours, and interchange approaches are adjusted locally to
keep capsules compact. Paths join at station centres and animate by opening section.
The pre-2005 Yongsan branch joins the existing Line 1 track at Hoegi even before the station opens;
its later, separate service uses an offset platform. Detached transfer markers have clear gaps,
and Seoul Station's walking connector follows each dated capsule centre, underneath the markers.

The background is **present-day geography at every date**, including reclaimed coastlines.
Seoul Special City is the own-land area; Incheon, Gyeonggi and all other territory use the outside
shade. The Han, Bukhan, Namhan, Imjin, Hantan and substantial connecting waterways remain
continuous; selected urban tributaries and large reservoirs provide context. Small ponds,
minor drainage, marine boundary polygons and coastline-sized administrative outlines are omitted.
The enlarged canvas permits the full network to fit clear of the laptop overlays after zooming out
and panning, independently of the close opening camera.

Route distances use published line/station tables, with shared passenger corridors counted for
each displayed line as elsewhere in the app. Suin–Bundang includes the 2.4 km Cheongnyangni branch
in addition to the commonly quoted 104.5 km Wangsimni–Incheon route. Gyeongui–Jungang includes its
Seoul and Dorasan branches. Opening-section distances are apportioned by mapped track length and
rounded to tenths, with the final section reconciled to the route total; historical kilometre values
are therefore estimates, not surveyed stage lengths.

This is a metropolitan **build history**, not every conventional-rail predecessor or operational
change. Line 1 is used as the continuous identity for its through-running metro/KNR service; the
older national-railway map branding is not separately modelled. Historical romanization revisions
and secondary/sponsored station subtitles are not exhaustively dated. Current alignments remain
for minor platform relocations (including the Gyeongui platforms at Seoul Station in 2017);
Bojeong's materially different former passenger branch is explicitly represented. These limitations
must not be described as a complete record of every historical railway name or platform movement.

The header logo is the Seoul Metro emblem from [Seoul Metro's Commons SVG](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seoul_Metro.svg),
cropped without stretching; it stands for the whole network (spec §1). The homepage preview is
generated from the latest active tracks only.

Station tooltips use the operator keys `metro` (Seoul Metro, also the fallback), `korail`,
`incheon`, `gimpo`, `arex`, `neotrans` and `maglev`. Seohae stations use `korail`, which operates
the line; Line 9, Ui–Sinseol, Sillim and GTX-A stations, which have no suitable text-free operator
symbol, keep the Seoul Metro fallback. The one handover is Line 7's Kkachiul – Bupyeong-gu Office
section, `metro` → `incheon` on 2022-01-01 (above). Each symbol is a text-free vector with editor
metadata removed and a `viewBox` set:

- Korail (`korail.svg`): the blue symbol of Korail's logo, cropped by its `viewBox`; the source
  file was not recorded.
- Incheon Transit (`incheon.svg`): [the operator's official SVG](https://www.ictr.or.kr/main/img/main2025/logo.svg)
  with its lettering removed ([symbol description](https://www.ictr.or.kr/foreign/eng/introduction/ci.jsp)).
- Gimpo Goldline (`gimpo.svg`): [the operator's official SVG](https://gimpogoldline.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Gimpo-Goldline_logo-1.svg),
  keeping the three symbol paths without lettering ([CI guide](https://gimpogoldline.com/?page_id=424)).
- Shinbundang (`neotrans.svg`): [NeoTrans logo](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NeoTrans_logo.svg), public
  domain, NeoTrans Co., Ltd.
- AREX (`arex.svg`): [AREX line icon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Seoul_Metro_Line_Arex.svg) by
  Chugun, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). The company logo is only
  published with lettering.
- Incheon Airport Maglev (`maglev.svg`): [line icon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Incheon_Airport_Maglev_Line.svg)
  by 夜月辰星, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). The operator's
  (Incheon International Airport Corporation) symbol is non-free.

## Geography and artwork: shared limitations

[OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) provide the modern mapped alignments linked above. The listed object IDs were recovered from the earlier geographic research; their live versions may change. Use the object history or a dated snapshot when reproducing an edit. These are crowdsourced spatial checks, not railway engineering certification or proof of historical opening dates.

The original supplied SVG and later adjustments are separate layers of provenance. A Commons licence applies to its identified artwork, not automatically to every later background, logo or geometry addition. Follow the linked file pages for the full attribution/file history. Exact original source revisions remain an explicit gap where they could not be recovered; a visually similar map is not sufficient attribution.

The maps deliberately simplify curves, parallel tracks and interchange capsules. Marker `id`s are repository identifiers, not official station codes. Colours may be inherited or adapted. Neither identifier spelling, symbol shape nor a tiny local display offset needs a historical event, but the station identity and line membership they represent do.

### Length reconciliation still required

- The line tables show **stored** active kilometre sums, not a claim that every figure was obtained directly from a primary source.
- Check each opening section against its published _operating_ length; project length can include unopened stations, sidings, depots or future extensions.
- Preserve the source precision before rounding to the SVG’s one decimal. When a sourced total is split between paths solely for animation/relocation/line reassignment, record the allocation method rather than presenting each split as independently measured.
- Historical KCR/Light Rail estimates, Tokyo shared corridors, Taipei differing historical section figures and Guangzhou Line 12’s 27.9/28.8 km discrepancy particularly need this treatment. A matching modern total cannot validate all earlier totals.
- Station counts are derived from the spec’s identities and simplification policy. They will not always equal an operator’s published “stations”, which may count interchange platforms once per line or include all intermediate LRT/tram stops.

## Map geography normalization

This log covers the twelve systems present in September 2026 before Seoul was added; Seoul describes its geography in its own section. Xi'an (added 2026-09-27) was built directly to these rules and is summarised in the tables below and [its section](#xian). Taipei's canvas was re-extended later (see its section).

### Current preservation policy (supersedes the intermediate rebuilds below)

The enlarged canvases and zoom limits are retained. The original geography from `c4fe500` is
preserved in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Guangfo, Taipei, Singapore and Tokyo.
All original path data and nested transforms remain intact; land fills are updated only for
correct administrative shading. The original artwork
is clipped to its original canvas and placed above the expanded geography. A land backing prevents
new background features showing through previously empty parts of that original artwork.

Only restrained additions are made inside those maps:

- **Shanghai:** Suzhou Creek/Wusong River and Dishui Lake; Dazhi River's continuation across the old eastern edge.
- **Shenzhen:** Dasha River; Tiegang, Xili, Shiyan, Shenzhen and Guangming reservoirs; Longgang River's continuation across the old eastern edge.
- **Guangfo:** the Beijiang gap at the original northwestern corner.
- **Hangzhou:** continuations of East Tiaoxi, the second canal channel, Hangyong and Xiaocao canals, and Puyang River across the old canvas edges; the missing Xixiao connecting reach and western Beitang reach to its mapped intake.
- **Taipei:** Maling Creek's continuation across the old eastern edge.
- **Tokyo:** Kanda, Ayase and Shingashi rivers, plus the short Nakagawa gap at the old northern edge.
- **Hong Kong and Singapore:** retain their original interior geography.

The added waterways use the September 23 OSM extracts and the existing coordinate fits, with
mapped banks where available and a thin centreline symbol where banks are absent. Continuations reuse
the already-curated banks and exclude existing water, allowing for small cartographic offsets.
Their outlines stop at existing water rather than adding duplicate banks or bars across confluences.
Small side-drain networks are excluded from these additions.
Suzhou Creek's Jiangsu reach was present but hidden underneath the preserved land shapes; its
addition now paints above the original fills, with only its exposed banks outlined. This also
removes the old Huangpu bank stroke across the tributary mouth without altering either original
path. The upstream Wusong/Suzhou identity
is also described by [Shanghai's government](https://service.shanghai.gov.cn/sheninfo/specialdetail.aspx?Id=da509036-d8fa-48d5-af6b-81ce21db55ab).
The continuity audit checked all twelve systems, including 31 selected river crossings of the old
canvas edges. It addresses clipped/hidden continuations, not every minor waterway omitted from the
original maps. Original path geometry, railway data, expanded bounds and runtime remain intact.
The original Pudong shoreline is restored; the intermediate tidal-flat treatment does not replace it.
Administrative land shading applies to **all twelve systems**, including the preserved interiors.
The boundaries are Hong Kong SAR, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Guangzhou + Foshan, Taipei +
New Taipei + Taoyuan, Singapore and Tokyo Metropolis; the four reworked maps use Beijing, Chengdu
and Chongqing municipalities and, for Nanjing, Jiangsu province. The existing OSM administrative polygons and coordinate fits supply these boundaries.
Tokyo uses full relation [1543125](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/1543125), version 384
(2026-09-20), because its offshore members prevent the regional extract assembling a complete area.

All eight preserved maps use solid fills and boundary overlays for administrative shading.
Full-map paint patterns were removed after zoom tests exposed expensive WebKit repaints in all
eight, especially Hong Kong and Tokyo. Overlays follow the existing polygons or clip to the original
Bezier curves; original coastline strokes remain on top. This keeps continuous shading without
altering shorelines, water fills or zoom behaviour. The four reworked maps already use solid fills.

**Beijing, Chengdu, Chongqing and Nanjing** are explicitly exempt from preservation. Their backgrounds
use the reworked, less cluttered geography: principal connected waterways, substantial lakes and
reservoirs, and administrative outside-land colours (Nanjing's own land is all of Jiangsu). Beijing/Chengdu/Chongqing lose minor ponds
and side drains; Nanjing gains useful Qinhuai/Yangtze, lake and regional-waterway context. Original
railway geometry and the expanded bounds remain unchanged in all twelve maps.

### Confluence and contextual-rail audit (2026-09-25)

This follow-up checked all twelve maps for old-edge railway cutoffs, waterway name changes,
shoreline seams, detail selection and administrative shading. Corrections are limited to:

| Map       | Correction and source geometry                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Hong Kong | Append XRL beyond the enlarged northern edge along [OSM relation 9405634](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/9405634), through Shenzhen toward Shenzhen North. Preserve the existing path prefix and tangent, West Kowloon terminal, opening date and Hong Kong-only `data-km="25.7"`. The [LegCo alignment paper](https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr16-17/english/panels/tp/tp_rdp/papers/tp_rdp20161209cb4-243-9-e.pdf) documents the Shenzhen/Futian–Longhua route.                                                                                                            |

The [Shanghai river register](https://www.shanghai.gov.cn/nw5558/20200905/0001-5558_352.html) identifies Wusong–Suzhou's endpoint as Huangpu.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Hangzhou  | Join Hangyong Canal through Xixiao River using ways 1221899641, 651959787 and 651959786. Add only Beitang's western reach from the Xiaocao junction to the mapped intake, using part of 113467368 and ways 1484314077–1484314078. The intake/culvert is not redrawn as an open Qiantang confluence. [Hangzhou's canal project report](https://epb.hangzhou.gov.cn/module/download/downfile.jsp?classid=0&filename=f8a25ba95b544721aab985a4da50f79c.pdf) documents the Puyang–Xixiao route.                                                                                     |

[Shenzhen's water authority](https://swj.sz.gov.cn/gkmlpt/content/5/5666/post_5666484.html) identifies Longgang as the upper Long–Dan river reach.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Tokyo     | Join the Tsurumi reaches tagged Yamoto (`谷本川`), ways 90332617, 1184496059, 1184496061 and 1392124883, plus short connector 148068758, in the expanded western margin. These join existing depicted reaches; surrounding tributaries are excluded.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

[Chongqing's river account](https://gxq.cq.gov.cn/hbslgg/202007/P020200724319866874079.pdf) describes the route through Longfengqiao to the Jialing mouth.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Nanjing   | Close the Baishitian connection (1122943982) and canal gaps on 71187259. Restore the unnamed reach 106061879 and Zhongshan junction 903408515, with Lishui ways 36829414, 586775002 and 400809820 connecting the isolated upper fragments to Qinhuai. Restore Jiajiang (159868004–159868005) using bank relation 2538928: this substantial Yangtze side channel separates Jiangxinzhou from the mainland. The [Nanjing government’s crossing description](https://www.nanjing.gov.cn/msxx/202510/t20251024_5675704.html) distinguishes Jiajiang from the main Yangtze channel. |
| Taipei    | Add a local Dahan River bank join at the original western canvas edge, following the mapped bend around the island. Preserve the original interior paths; draw only exposed banks over the seam.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

The island/channel follow-up also compared unnamed and differently named branches between
already depicted water areas across all twelve maps. Bank polygons restore Huangshali and nearby
delta connections in Shenzhen; Xihai, Dongping and Xinkai connections in Guangfo; two short
lake/channel connections in Shanghai's added western margin; Fenshui and Yaowan reaches in
Hangzhou; an exposed side channel in Tokyo; the Fu River reach in Chengdu; Baihe/Xinhe reaches
in Beijing; the Qu River bend and a Yangtze side channel in Chongqing; and omitted connected
regional channels in Nanjing. Hong Kong gains one short delta connection in its expanded margin.
These additions follow source water polygons, not straight endpoint bridges. Bank-less routes and covered channels are not automatically converted into open water;
the source-bank pass adds no connecting channels in Taipei or Singapore.

All twelve maps also receive finer source-bank detail within the existing added-water footprint,
using the original opening scale rather than the expanded canvas to set simplification tolerance.
This refines depicted bends without selecting more tiny lakes or surrounding drainage networks.
The eight preserved interiors retain their original path data and transforms.

Source way IDs refer to the September 23 Geofabrik/OSM extracts used for the expansion. Added
reaches reuse mapped bank polygons where available, with the existing thin centreline convention
elsewhere. No isolated lakes, surrounding side-drain networks or covered Beijing moat were added.
Original artwork omissions and genuine headwaters are not automatically treated as broken joins.
Preserved original path data and transforms, station data, dates, distances, canvas bounds and
runtime/configuration code are unchanged; XRL's appended continuation is the sole railway edit.

Final bank-detail validation: all twelve map-data checks and administrative-color probes pass.
The eight protected interiors retain their original path data and transforms; canvas bounds and
railway data are preserved except for the documented XRL extension. A production-build check
across twelve maps, Chromium/WebKit, both themes and three zoom levels sampled 5,184 frames:
maximum mean frame time 17.1 ms, one frame above 32 ms, and no browser errors. This is a local
rendering benchmark, not a guarantee for every device. The production build passes.

Validation of this preservation pass: all eight original geography trees match their baseline
path data and transforms (land-fill references change for shading). The twelve map-data checkers pass; SVG bounds and
railway nodes match the pre-pass versions, and runtime/configuration code is unchanged. All twelve
maps render in both themes. The four reworked maps pass checks of 94 substantial/landmark lakes
and their selected principal-river centrelines at overview tolerance. Production build passes.

### Regression audit after the geography expansion (2026-09-25)

Reviewed Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei, Singapore, Tokyo, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Guangfo,
Chengdu, Beijing, Nanjing and Chongqing. The additional correction is limited to Beijing's
and Nanjing's `inland-water` paths: some source polygons combine `natural=water`,
`landuse=farmland` and `intermittent=yes`. Their flood-retention fields were incorrectly
painted as permanent lakes. Remove those field surfaces and their residual outlines while
retaining independently mapped water bodies and river courses within them.

- **Beijing's expanded surroundings:** ways 1181920553, 1195186174–1195186175,
  1195186688–1195186689, 1195288131, 1195594923–1195594927 and 1195903054.
  These include Yongding and Zhaowang flood-retention areas. The
  [Beijing water authority's Yongding plan](https://swj.beijing.gov.cn/zwgk/ghjhzj/202107/P020210705624970672074.pdf)
  distinguishes river, inundation and bank-protection areas and their mixed land uses.
- **Nanjing's expanded northwestern surroundings:** relation 6905928 and ways
  471512676 and 471512718, near the Huai River/Shouxian floodplain. The
  [Shouxian land-use plan](https://www.shouxian.gov.cn/public/118322767/1260264458.html)
  distinguishes flood-retention areas from river channels;
  [Shouxihu Farm's account](https://www.ahnk.com.cn/display.php?id=16720)
  documents the extensive farmland there. This does not remove genuine lakes or reservoirs.

No matching painted flood-field issue was found in the other ten maps. Source-tag checks
also distinguish genuine round reservoirs/ponds from the unwanted marine-area outlines.
Original geography, railways, timeline data, camera configuration and runtime code are
unchanged in this audit. In particular, Nanjing's restored Jiajiang side channel and upper
Qinhuai connections remain intact.

Validation:

- All twelve map-data checkers and administrative-colour probes pass; added geography has
  valid polygon rings and no detached marine-water overlays.
- All eight protected interiors retain their original geometry. A rendered comparison at
  2,200 pixels wide found no erased original water interiors, excluding shoreline antialiasing.
- All 72 viewport checks pass: five laptop sizes and one mobile size per system. Opening
  transforms and maximum zoom match the baseline; pan limits retain the enlarged canvas.
  Latest station markers clear expanded panels at minimum zoom in all 60 laptop checks.
  Complete active line-path bounds also clear the panels in a separate 60-case check,
  excluding XRL's deliberately off-canvas contextual continuation.
- Search, tooltip dismissal, preserved highlight/search magnification, and date/playback/
  highlight preservation after resize pass on every system. Repeated theme toggles restore
  the same light-mode geography colours. No browser errors were observed.
- The older ignored local test scripts were updated for the current playback settings and
  test mocks; 29 playback, transition and search tests pass, including the original Airport
  Express dash behavior. Lint and the production build pass.
- A fresh final-asset Chromium/WebKit run covers all twelve systems in both themes at
  three zoom levels: 144 combinations, 5,184 sampled frames, maximum mean 17.1 ms,
  maximum 95th-percentile 21 ms, one frame above 32 ms, and no browser errors.
  These are local rendering measurements, not a performance guarantee for every device.

One pre-existing schematic discrepancy remains intentionally unchanged: AsiaWorld-Expo's
marker centre slightly overlaps the original shoreline. Both baseline and current rendered
maps show the same overlap. These checks establish regression coverage against the artwork
and selected geographic sources, not exhaustive real-world or historical completeness.

The earlier sections below record intermediate datasets, corrections and validation results; their
whole-map regeneration and coverage figures do not describe the preserved final interiors.

September 24, 2026: all twelve canvases were extended on all four sides. The original
`initialBounds` and `initialView` still determine the opening framing and maximum zoom;
the expanded SVG `viewBox` determines the minimum zoom and pan limits. Railway coordinates,
identities, labels and distances are unchanged, except for the Jinshan completion noted below.
These are **present-day backgrounds throughout playback**, not historical coastlines.

### Data and coordinate alignment

Water, coastline ways and administrative polygons come from © OpenStreetMap contributors,
[ODbL 1.0](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), via Geofabrik's September 23, 2026 snapshots:

- [China regional extracts](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/china.html): Guangdong (including
  Hong Kong), Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Hebei (including Beijing), Sichuan and Chongqing.
- [Taiwan](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/taiwan.html),
  [Kanto](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/japan/kanto.html), and
  [Malaysia–Singapore–Brunei](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/malaysia-singapore-brunei.html).

Existing WGS84-to-SVG coordinate fits were retained for Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei, Tokyo,
Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Guangfo. Guangfo's fit includes the existing artwork's 550-unit horizontal
translation; this corrects the reference transform, not the railway drawing. Median station-control
residuals are respectively 2.37, 2.28, 4.91, 2.32, 1.03, 1.68 and 1.48 SVG units. These fits reproduce
geographic artwork with local schematic offsets; they do not establish survey-grade platform positions.
Singapore uses a robust affine fit to 34 matched station controls (median residual 7.22 SVG units,
about one pixel at its original laptop opening scale).

Beijing and Nanjing retain EPSG:32650 at 20 metres per SVG unit, and Xi'an uses EPSG:32649 at the same scale with the Geofabrik [Shaanxi](https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/china/shaanxi.html) extract of the same date and Xi'an's municipal relation 3226004; Chongqing retains EPSG:32648
at 18 metres per unit. Chengdu retains its station-calibrated Web Mercator fit and the existing
1552.494-unit west-extension translation. Administrative relations retained are Hong Kong 913110,
Shanghai 913067, Beijing 912940, Chengdu 2110264, Chongqing 913069, Jiangsu 913012 and Singapore 536780. The Sham Chun/Shenzhen border river retains bank polygon relation 9791660, exempt from
small-water filtering. Boundaries divide land colours only; mapped coastlines determine land versus sea.

### Geography re-audit and corrections

The first normalization pass was too aggressive. Its `2 × area / perimeter` filter discarded
branching reservoirs and narrow bank sections, including unnamed sections of principal rivers.
An exact-name filter also missed the English-labelled Huangpu bank relation **197358**. Passing
the map-data checker did not detect these geographic omissions.

The revised pass assesses whole lakes before clipping, retains lakes/reservoirs of at least
100 overview pixels² plus named urban landmarks, and selects principal river corridors using
both names and spatial matches to their bank polygons. This includes significant navigation
canals, not just features tagged `water=river`. Unnamed banks are unioned with their adjoining
sections before simplification. Small ponds and minor irrigation channels remain omitted.
Perimeter/width is no longer used to reject lakes or principal bank sections. Other minor river
features are screened separately; a large connected irrigation grid is not automatically retained.
Shoreline simplification is reduced from 0.4 to **0.2 overview pixels**, with topology and holes
preserved. Centreline symbols are restricted to missing-bank stretches instead of widening the
entire river over mapped banks.

**Taihu at the first expansion (before the further expansion below):** relation **1126533** has identical full geometry in the Jiangsu and Zhejiang
extracts. Shanghai's expanded viewport contains about **1.9%** of its water area—the eastern fringe;
Nanjing's contains about **53.6%**. The rest lies outside those canvases, rather than being deleted
from the lake polygon. Against the projected source, the simplified visible water area omitted is
approximately **0.17%** in Shanghai and **0.07%** in Nanjing. These are geometry comparisons, not
an independent survey. Nearby Dianshan, Yangcheng, Cheng and other lakes are separate features;
the [Taihu Basin Authority's lake inventory](https://www.tba.gov.cn/slbthlyglj/lygk/content/3035596f-70fb-426e-9011-72a20188926e.html)
provides an independent check of that distinction.

- [Hong Kong WSD: Tai Lam Chung Reservoir](https://www.wsd.gov.hk/en/customer-services/other-customer-services/fishing-in-reservoirs/brief-introduction-of-reservoirs/tai-lam-chung-reservoir/index.html).
- [Singapore PUB: Jurong Lake](https://www.pub.gov.sg/Public/Places-of-Interest/Our-Reservoirs-and-Waterways/Jurong-Lake)
  and [reservoir/waterway inventory](https://www.pub.gov.sg/Public/Places-of-Interest/Our-Reservoirs-and-Waterways).
- [Tokyo's river inventory](https://www.kensetsu.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/river/kanri) and
  [bridge/waterway inventory](https://www.kensetsu.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/content/000060891.pdf).
- [Chongqing government: Yulin River](https://www.cq.gov.cn/zwgk/zfxxgkml/zdlyxxgk/stbh/hjbh/202404/t20240429_13169521.html).

These official sources corroborate feature identity and connectivity; the detailed bank coordinates
still come from the OSM snapshot above. The audit compared water polygons, checked duplicate
relations across neighbouring extracts, inspected coastlines/islands and rendered all twelve maps
in light and dark themes. It did not independently survey every bank or validate seasonal water levels.

That re-audit’s coverage check compared **534 map/feature pairs**: water bodies of at least 150 overview
pixels² with at least one visible pixel², plus the named Huangpu/Suzhou features. After allowing the
0.2-pixel simplification tolerance and coordinate rounding, none had more than one pixel² of
uncovered source water. This checks substantial-feature omissions against the chosen dataset;
it does not certify all smaller waterways or the dataset itself. All **3,253 serialized polygon
rings** are valid, and all twelve map-data checkers pass. Comparing each SVG with the start of this
re-audit confirms that everything outside `#geography`, including the viewBox, is unchanged.

Station-center checks flag small water overlaps at AsiaWorld-Expo (0.49 SVG units),
Nakano-fujimichō (0.52), Changlingpi (0.79), Haixinsha (0.02) and Anheqiao Bei (0.21).
AsiaWorld-Expo and Anheqiao Bei also overlap water in the pre-expansion artwork. Changlingpi
and Anheqiao Bei's projected source station points themselves fall just inside the source-derived
water rendering. These are alignment/data limitations, not proof that the riverbank should move;
station points can also differ from a platform footprint. Railway coordinates and source banks
were not nudged to conceal the flags. The station-control residuals above remain relevant when
viewing individual markers at high zoom.

Follow-up: removed three redundant marine-water outlines—Crooked Harbour (OSM way 675102262)
from the Hong Kong and Shenzhen maps, and Rocky Harbour (way 676971270) from Hong Kong.
Their circular outlines lay entirely inside the existing sea fill, not along physical shorelines.
The earlier inland-water coverage check missed this distinction. Marine components are now
excluded from the additional water outline layer, and coverage checks include the sea layer.
Round inland lakes/reservoirs are not removed merely for being round.

uses the rendered panels and network bounds at five laptop sizes. It leaves at least 24 pixels
of clearance and checks both extremes of each constrained pan axis at minimum zoom, with
additional rounding/stroke slack. The full-view button is not required.

Validation: 60 laptop layouts (all twelve systems at 1280 × 720, 1280 × 800, 1366 × 768,
1440 × 900 and 1536 × 864); the normal minimum-zoom position and all four constrained pan
corners remain inside the measured clear area in every layout. All 60 opening transforms match
exactly. Mobile opening framing, light/dark rendering, polygon validity, unwanted marine overlays,
unchanged railway data and the twelve map-data checkers also pass. The final coverage check
compares 478 map/feature pairs (whole water bodies of at least 150 overview pixels², with a
visible portion of at least 1 pixel², plus the named Huangpu/Suzhou/Taihu checks). None has more
than 1 pixel² missing beyond simplification tolerance. Sea and inland water are checked together
so redundant marine outlines are not rewarded as “coverage.” This tests the selected OSM snapshot,
not exhaustive real-world completeness; small omitted waterways remain intentional.

### Jinshan Railway cutoff exposed by expansion

The old Shanghai drawing stopped south of Yexie and omitted Tinglin, Jinshan Yuanqu and
Jinshanwei. The enlarged canvas exposed that cutoff. The existing 2012 opening path now follows
mapped passenger tracks to Jinshanwei, with those three station markers added from **2012-09-28**.
The original path north of the cutoff, opening event and **56.4 km** value remain intact. This adds
three stations to statistics/search from that date; it is an explicit data correction, not a claimed
behavior-neutral change. Pre-2012 freight history is outside this map's Jinshan commuter-service scope.

Sources: the [2012 opening report](https://news.sina.com.cn/o/2012-09-18/150125200013.shtml),
[Jinshan Yuanqu station history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinshan_Yuanqu_railway_station),
and the [Jinshan district's 2025 timetable and fare map](https://www.shanghai.gov.cn/nw17239/20250103/d4782b40a6f74ef5a5605f102b2bf984.html).
The continuation geometry uses the same Shanghai coordinate fit and the regional OSM railway ways.

Validation of the first expansion: all twelve spec checkers pass. All latest-date drawn networks fit at minimum zoom in
1366 × 768, 1440 × 900 and 1536 × 864 viewports (36 checks); overlays can be hidden with the
existing full-view control. Opening transforms match the prior framing within 0.001 pixel across
those sizes and 390 × 844 mobile (48 comparisons). Extreme pans remain clamped at minimum and
maximum zoom; the maximum zoom and search magnification are preserved. Light/dark rendering,
shoreline alignment, polygon-ring validity, lint and the production build were checked.

## Updating the register

For a new or corrected fact, update the relevant event row **and** the applicable line/station/geometry entry. Record the actual passenger date, source publication date, exact article/PDF page or chronology entry, and what the source establishes. Prefer a stable article URL over a homepage/search result. Preserve an archive URL for an inaccessible original, and label a reported/approximate date honestly.

Do not promote a recovered citation to “verified” without reading the relevant passage. Resolve mixed rows description by description; e.g. a line-opening announcement may substantiate the route but say nothing about the English name rollout or whether a transfer is within the paid area. Check SVG/legend boundaries against the revised event date after a data correction.

This register is documentation only; it is not imported by the application. It does not add sources/network/audit JSON to the runtime data model.
